disclaimer: A public finding aid for names a B2B company might hold or claim. Listing here is not an endorsement and not legal advice. Regulations are not vendor certifications. Verify the live certificate, Marketplace listing, or statute; do not rely on a trust-page badge. kind 'authorization' is used for government ATO / Marketplace programs (FedRAMP, GovRAMP, TX-RAMP) in addition to the core kinds.

attestations.name: AIUC-1
attestations.issuer: Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company; accredited auditor issues the certificate
attestations.eli5: An independent audit that an AI agent was tested against a quarterly-updated enterprise standard for security, safety, and reliability. It is not ISO 42001 and not a government license.
attestations.elaborate: AIUC-1 is a certification against the Artificial Intelligence Underwriting Company’s standard for AI agents. The six pillars are security, safety, reliability, accountability, data and privacy, and societal impact. The company publishes the standard; an accredited auditor issues the certificate. Schellman became the first accredited auditor in February 2026. The standard refreshes quarterly on a fixed calendar (15 January, 15 April, 15 July, 15 October). The edition current on this file is 15 July 2026. It operationalizes ISO 42001, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, MITRE ATLAS, and the OWASP LLM Top 10 into testable agent practices and technical tests. A typical audit runs four to eight weeks: scoping the named agents, evidence collection, technical evaluation against adversarial scenarios, then the independent auditor’s opinion. To keep the mark, those agents are re-tested quarterly and the engagement is re-audited annually. Scope is usually named products or agent systems, not the whole firm. A certificate on a voice model is not evidence for a coding agent or an unlisted subsidiary. Buyers must read the report: which systems were in scope, which standard version, which practices were tested, and what was carved out. AIUC-1 is not ISO 42001. ISO 42001 certifies an AI management system (AIMS). AIUC-1 certifies that named agents were tested against this agent standard. It is not the NIST AI RMF; that framework issues no certificate. It is not an EU AI Act conformity assessment and not a government license. A logo on a trust page is not the report. Typical evidence is the certificate and the report under NDA. Absence of the mark is not evidence of no agent testing; presence is not evidence your use case was in scope.

attestations.name: Binding Corporate Rules
attestations.issuer: Lead supervisory authority / EDPB cooperation under GDPR Articles 46–47
attestations.eli5: A company's own internal privacy rules, approved by a European regulator, so the group can move personal data among its affiliates. Rare, slow, and real. Not a product certificate for a SaaS you buy.
attestations.elaborate: Binding Corporate Rules are a GDPR Article 47 transfer mechanism: a group's legally binding internal policies for international transfers, approved through the cooperation procedure with a lead supervisory authority and the EDPB. There are controller BCRs and processor BCRs. Approval is public enough that a buyer can often verify the group and the lead authority. BCRs are not a security certification of a named SaaS product. They authorize intra-group transfers that match the approved scope. They do not replace a DPA with the customer and do not approve transfers to unaffiliated subprocessors — those still need another Article 46 tool. Typical evidence is the approval and the BCR summary. BCRs are uncommon relative to SCCs; their presence is meaningful for large groups and meaningless if the product's subprocessors sit outside the group. Score them as a real, regulator-reviewed mechanism, not as FedRAMP. The EDPB publishes information on approved BCRs. Approval takes time and political coordination among authorities; that cost is why BCRs are a large-group tool. Processor BCRs help a group that offers processing to many controllers. They still need a controller-processor contract with the customer. Intra-group subprocessors inside the BCR perimeter are the win. Outside processors need SCCs or another tool. A BCR application 'in progress' is not an approval. Do not accept a draft policy. Score an approved BCR as a meaningful transfer mechanism, stronger than a bare SCC claim because a supervisor reviewed it, still far below a security authorization. If the product's data leaves the group, the BCR does not follow it.

attestations.name: BSI C5
attestations.issuer: BSI (catalog); independent auditor issues the attestation
attestations.eli5: Germany's cloud-security criteria catalog from the BSI. An auditor writes a report, often like a SOC report. The BSI does not stamp your company. Customers are supposed to read the report.
attestations.elaborate: The Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue (C5) is published by Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI). Current widely used edition is C5:2020; BSI has been revising the catalog (including work toward a later edition). C5 is not a BSI-issued certificate. An independent auditor attests against the criteria, commonly under ISAE 3000, as Type 1 (design at a date) or Type 2 (operating effectiveness over a period). BSI states it does not select auditors or review reports; the customer must read the report. Criteria split into basic and additional requirements across 17 areas, mapped to ISO 27001 and other sources. German public-sector and, in health, statutory cloud rules have increasingly pointed at C5 Type 2 — verify the current legal pointer for your sector. C5 is not FedRAMP and not ISO 27001, though a combined C5/SOC 2 report is common. Typical evidence is the C5 attestation report under NDA. A logo is not the report. Prefer Type 2. Type 1 versus Type 2 is the same idea as SOC: prefer Type 2 covering a period. Combined C5 + SOC 2 reports are common and still have to be read as two criteria sets. Additional criteria above the basic set matter when the customer has a higher protection need. A report that carved out the region you will use is the wrong report. If a vendor only has ISO 27001 and says 'equivalent to C5,' that is a mapping claim. Score the attestation, not the mapping. C5:2020 is the edition most reports still name.

attestations.name: CAIQ
attestations.issuer: Cloud Security Alliance
attestations.eli5: A long yes/no questionnaire CSA wrote so buyers can ask cloud vendors the same security questions. Filling it out is not a certification.
attestations.elaborate: The Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire is CSA's question set derived from the Cloud Controls Matrix. The version submitted to the STAR Registry is the STAR Level 1 Security Questionnaire (CAIQ v4 / v4.1 as specified by CSA). It is a questionnaire, not a certification. Providers answer it for the registry or send it to customers. Answers are claims unless backed by Level 2 or another audit. Typical evidence is the completed CAIQ or the STAR Registry item. Do not treat a filled CAIQ as equivalent to SOC 2. SIG is a different questionnaire family from Shared Assessments; do not merge them. CAIQ versions and STAR-submissible versions have been split in CSA's downloads: the reference CAIQ in the CCM bundle is not always the file CSA wants in the registry. Use the STAR Level 1 Security Questionnaire if the point is publication. Question IDs change between v3 and v4; an old completed CAIQ is painful to map. Shared Assessments SIG is a different taxonomy — do not merge answer files. Some GRC platforms ingest CAIQ as a standard. That convenience is not assurance. Typical buyer use is to pre-fill a questionnaire. Typical misuse is to call the completed file a certification. This register's kind field exists so that misuse can be detected. Weight stays at questionnaire level.

attestations.name: CCPA / CPRA
attestations.issuer: State of California; California Privacy Protection Agency and Attorney General
attestations.eli5: California's consumer privacy law, as expanded by the CPRA. If a company is in scope, it must follow the statute. There is no California privacy certificate for vendors.
attestations.elaborate: The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act (Proposition 24, operative for most provisions in 2023), is state law. The California Privacy Protection Agency and the Attorney General enforce. It creates consumer rights and business duties for entities that meet thresholds or process data in specified ways. It is not a certification. A 'CCPA compliant' badge is a claim. Service-provider and contractor contract language matters more than a logo. The CPRA is the amendment; modern references should be to the amended CCPA, not to a separate certificate called CPRA. This is not GDPR. Typical evidence is contract terms and a privacy notice, not a cert PDF. Weight is low for the same reason as GDPR: nearly everyone in a B2B directory claims it, and it is not third-party assurance. Thresholds (revenue, records sold or shared, and percentage of revenue from selling or sharing) decide who is a 'business.' Employee and B2B personal information, once exempt, were pulled into the amended Act on a published timetable. Service-provider contracts have statutory content. The CPPA issues regulations that change operational detail (risk assessments, cybersecurity audits, automated decision-making) on their own calendar — do not freeze a 2023 blog into this row. There is no CPPA certification for a SaaS. A 'Do Not Sell' link is a notice feature, not an audit. If the only California artifact is a privacy policy, you have a policy. Score the statute low. When a deal is actually in scope, the contract and the vendor's delete/export machinery matter more than this encyclopedia's weight field.

attestations.name: CIS Controls
attestations.issuer: Center for Internet Security
attestations.eli5: A prioritized list of security safeguards from the Center for Internet Security, in implementation groups. Anyone can adopt them. CIS does not certify your whole company for listing them.
attestations.elaborate: The CIS Critical Security Controls are a prioritized set of safeguards published by the Center for Internet Security. Version 8 / 8.1 organizes controls into Implementation Groups IG1, IG2, and IG3. Organizations adopt them as a baseline. CIS offers related products (CSAT self-assessment, CIS Benchmarks for hardening, and some independently assessed Benchmark programs). There is no general 'CIS Controls certified company' mark equivalent to ISO 27001. A trust page that says 'CIS Controls aligned' is a mapping claim. Typical evidence is a scored CSAT or an independent assessment against a stated IG, not a CIS corporate seal. Benchmarks (for example CIS Amazon Linux) are product-hardening artifacts, not an organization certificate. Score the framework low unless a third party tested a stated IG. IG1 is basic hygiene, IG2 is an operational security program, IG3 is a more mature set. CIS Benchmarks are configuration recommendations for named platforms and are independently listed when a product is certified against a Benchmark — that is a product hardening mark, not an organization CIS Controls certificate. Do not file a CIS-CAT score as a company certification. Do not file 'we implement CIS' as equal to ISO 27001. This row exists because the string is everywhere. Typical evidence, if any, is an internal score or a third-party gap assessment naming the version and IG. Without that, weight is a mapping claim. Pair with SOC 2 or 27001 when those exist and treat CIS as the vocabulary of prioritized safeguards.

attestations.name: CMMC Level 1
attestations.issuer: U.S. Department of Defense; status posted in SPRS
attestations.eli5: The basic Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification level for contractors that handle ordinary federal contract information. Today it is a self-assessment, posted in a government system.
attestations.elaborate: CMMC Level 1 (Self) is defined in 32 CFR Part 170. It requires the 15 basic safeguarding requirements in FAR 52.204-21 for Federal Contract Information (FCI). The organization seeking assessment performs an annual self-assessment and posts results in the Supplier Performance Risk System (SPRS), with an affirmation. Plans of action and milestones are not permitted at Level 1. This is not a C3PAO certificate. It is not protection of CUI (that is Level 2). It is not NIST SP 800-171. Phase 1 of CMMC implementation, in effect since November 2025, includes Level 1 self-assessment as a condition of award where designated. Typical evidence is an SPRS status the prime or the Department can see — not a PDF badge on a marketing site. A public 'CMMC L1 certified' claim without SPRS is unverifiable. Do not confuse this with Cyber Essentials or CIS IG1. FAR 52.204-21 is fifteen basic requirements, not a full 800-171 program. Companies sometimes slap a CMMC L1 badge on a commercial SaaS that never sees FCI. If there is no DoD contract flow-down, the badge is theatre. SPRS entries are not public, so a buyer who is not the government or a prime has to take the vendor's word or ask for a redacted affirmation. That is a real verification gap. Do not treat a commercial questionnaire mapped to the fifteen as a CMMC status. Level 1 does not permit POA&Ms; either the requirements are met or the status is not there. Annual reaffirmation is part of the rule. Expired affirmation, expired status.

attestations.name: CMMC Level 2
attestations.issuer: U.S. Department of Defense / The Cyber AB (for C3PAO assessments)
attestations.eli5: The CMMC level for contractors that handle controlled unclassified information. It maps to NIST 800-171. A third-party certificate exists, but as of July 2026 the Department paused requiring those third-party assessments.
attestations.elaborate: CMMC Level 2 is the CUI level. The security requirement set is the 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 Revision 2, as required by DFARS 252.204-7012. Two statuses exist in the rule: Level 2 (Self), a self-assessment posted to SPRS every three years with annual affirmation, and Level 2 (C3PAO), a third-party assessment by a Cyber AB-accredited C3PAO. On 13 July 2026 the Department of War announced immediate suspension of CMMC Phase II, which would have made C3PAO Level 2 a routine condition of award, and paused later phases. Phase I self-assessment requirements remain in place. Existing C3PAO certificates were not voided. Level 3 (DIBCAC, NIST SP 800-172) is out of scope for this entry and is also paused for new mandates. CMMC is not FedRAMP. Typical evidence for a C3PAO certificate is the Cyber AB / CMMC marketplace listing and SPRS status. Typical evidence for self is SPRS. A logo is not enough. DFARS 252.204-7012 safeguarding and incident reporting remain regardless of the Phase II pause. The July 2026 Phase II suspension is a Department memo and implementation pause, not a repeal of 32 CFR 170 or of DFARS 252.204-7012. Self-assessment at Level 2 remains a condition of award where designated. C3PAO certificates already issued remain useful to primes and in diligence. Do not tell a customer that CMMC 'went away.' Do not tell them a C3PAO assessment is currently required on every new DoD contract; as of this register it is not. Level 3 is a different assessment (DIBCAC, 800-172) and is not this row. A commercial SaaS that does not process CUI should not wear a CMMC L2 badge. Ask where CUI lives in that assessed boundary.

attestations.name: CSA Cloud Controls Matrix
attestations.issuer: Cloud Security Alliance
attestations.eli5: CSA's list of cloud security controls. It is the library behind STAR and CAIQ. A company can map to it. Mapping is not a certificate.
attestations.elaborate: The Cloud Controls Matrix is CSA's cloud security control framework. Current published editions in wide use are CCM v4 and v4.1 (CSA has published v4.1 with a transition path for STAR submissions). It organizes controls across cloud domains and maps to other standards. It is not a certification. STAR Level 1 and Level 2 use it. Buyers should not accept 'we follow CCM' as assurance. Typical evidence is a STAR Registry entry or an independent report that tested CCM controls. ISO 27017 and CCM overlap in topic, not in issuance. Score the framework low; score STAR Level 2 or ISO 27001 when those exist. CCM v4 / v4.1 organizes more than two hundred controls across on the order of seventeen domains (exact counts belong on the CSA artifact, not memorized from a blog). Mappings to ISO 27001, SOC 2, FedRAMP, and others are included in the download bundle and are CSA's mappings, not an auditor's opinion. Implementation and auditing guidelines exist. None of that is a certificate. A customer can require a vendor to complete CAIQ against CCM; that is procurement, not CSA STAR Level 2. This row lets a crawler attach the string 'CCM' without giving it STAR Level 2's weight. If both strings appear, score Level 2 when the registry says Level 2, and treat CCM as the library behind it.

attestations.name: CSA STAR Level 1
attestations.issuer: Cloud Security Alliance
attestations.eli5: A cloud company fills out the CSA questionnaire and publishes it in the STAR registry. Nobody independent had to audit it. Useful transparency, weak assurance.
attestations.elaborate: CSA STAR Level 1 is a self-assessment. The provider completes the Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ / STAR Level 1 Security Questionnaire) based on the Cloud Controls Matrix and submits it to the CSA STAR Registry. CSA may offer optional automated checks (Valid-AI-ted) on submissions; that is not a third-party audit of the cloud service. Level 1 is transparency, not certification. Anyone can publish a CAIQ. Buyers should open the registry entry, read the date, and treat answers as claims. Typical evidence is the public STAR Registry URL. STAR Level 2 is the audited tier. Do not score Level 1 as if it were ISO 27001 or SOC 2. The underlying questionnaire is also catalogued as caiq. Open the registry line: organization, service name, submission date, CCM/CAIQ version. Answers that say 'yes' to every control with no comments are as uninformative as empty cells. Some providers attach a CCM-based report instead of, or in addition to, a CAIQ; that is still Level 1 if it is self-produced. Valid-AI-ted, when used, is CSA's automated review of the questionnaire, not an on-site audit of the cloud. Annual refresh is expected; a 2019 CAIQ on CCM v3 is a relic. Level 1 is appropriate transparency for a small provider that has not yet paid for Level 2. It is not appropriate as the only cloud assurance on an enterprise deal. Score it like a completed SIG, plus the benefit of a public URL.

attestations.name: CSA STAR Level 2
attestations.issuer: Cloud Security Alliance (via accredited certification bodies or CPA firms)
attestations.eli5: A third party audits a cloud provider against the CSA cloud-control set, usually on top of ISO 27001 or SOC 2. Stronger than the self-filled Level 1 form.
attestations.elaborate: CSA STAR Level 2 is third-party assurance against the Cloud Controls Matrix. Two common shapes exist: STAR Certification, an extension of ISO/IEC 27001 performed by a certification body, and STAR Attestation, a SOC 2 engagement that includes CCM criteria, performed by a CPA firm. Both should be visible in the STAR Registry. Level 2 is not Level 1. Level 3 (continuous auditing) has been described by CSA for years and is rarely what a B2B buyer is looking at on a trust page; do not assume a vendor has it. STAR Certification generally expects an ISO 27001 ISMS. Typical evidence is the STAR Registry entry plus the ISO certificate or SOC 2/STAR attestation report. A self-published CAIQ is not Level 2. Score Level 2 with other independent cloud attestations, below FedRAMP. Ask which shape: STAR Certification (ISO path) or STAR Attestation (SOC 2 path). They are not the same PDF. The ISO path needs a certification body that offers the CCM extension; the SOC 2 path needs a CPA firm that included CCM criteria. Registry entries should say which. Continuous-monitoring Level 3 remains uncommon; if a vendor claims Level 3, demand the registry line before you score it, and do not invent a Level 3 row here without that evidence. STAR Level 2 still has a scope: one service, not the whole catalog. A hyperscaler's Level 2 does not cover an ISV running on top. Read the service name. Pair with the underlying ISO or SOC 2 report. That report is where exceptions live.

attestations.name: Cyber Essentials
attestations.issuer: UK National Cyber Security Centre; delivered via IASME consortium
attestations.eli5: A short UK government cyber hygiene scheme. The company answers questions about five basic controls. A person can get the badge without an on-site hack-test. Plus is the tested version.
attestations.elaborate: Cyber Essentials is a UK scheme owned by the National Cyber Security Centre and operated through the IASME consortium and licensed certification bodies. It covers five technical control themes: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection, and security update management. The base certificate is a self-assessment that is verified by a certification body; it is not a penetration test. UK government contracts often require at least Cyber Essentials. It is not ISO 27001 and not SOC 2. Typical evidence is the certificate and the listing on the NCSC/IASME registry. Validity is one year. Cyber Essentials Plus is a separate, hands-on assessed certificate. Do not score base CE as Plus. Scope (which legal entity and which network) matters; a group badge may not cover the product environment. The five themes are deliberately basic. Home-worker devices and cloud admin paths are common scope fights. A certificate that scoped only the London office network does not cover the AWS organization that runs the product. UK government supplier guidance has required CE for many contracts; some require Plus. IASME's registry is the lookup. A PDF without a registry match is suspect. CE is not Cyber Essentials Plus, not ISO 27001, not Cyber Essentials (Singapore), and not CIS IG1, though the hygiene ideas overlap. This register keeps the UK scheme only under this family. Score it as a small, real certificate. Do not let it stand in for SOC 2 on a U.S. enterprise questionnaire.

attestations.name: Cyber Essentials Plus
attestations.issuer: UK National Cyber Security Centre; delivered via IASME consortium
attestations.eli5: The tested version of Cyber Essentials. An assessor actually checks the five basic controls, including vulnerability scans. Still a hygiene certificate, not a full ISO audit.
attestations.elaborate: Cyber Essentials Plus adds an independent technical assessment to the Cyber Essentials control set, including vulnerability scanning of in-scope systems and checks that the five themes work in practice. It is still a bounded hygiene scheme, not an ISMS certificate and not a SOC 2. UK public-sector and some regulated buyers ask for Plus rather than the base badge. Typical evidence is the Plus certificate and registry listing. Validity is one year. A base Cyber Essentials certificate is not Plus. Scope limitations apply; a scan that excluded production cloud accounts is a problem. Score Plus above base CE and well below ISO 27001. The technical assessment will fail on missing patches, weak passwords, and unmanaged endpoints in scope. That is the value. It will not test application authorization logic or a multi-tenant isolation bug. Plus is still the five themes, tested. Some insurers and UK public buyers treat Plus as the minimum. A Plus certificate on a sister company is not yours. Check the legal name and the scope statement. One year, then reassess. If a vendor holds both CE and Plus, score Plus and do not double count. If they hold Plus and ISO 27001, score both; they answer different questions. This row is the hands-on UK hygiene mark. It is not a substitute for a Type II report.

attestations.name: DORA
attestations.issuer: European Union (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554); ESAs and national competent authorities
attestations.eli5: An EU law that says banks and other financial firms, and their important tech suppliers, must be operationally resilient. It is not a vendor certificate you can download.
attestations.elaborate: The Digital Operational Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554) has applied since 17 January 2025. It imposes ICT risk, incident, testing, and third-party duties on financial entities and, for critical ICT third-party providers, a Union-level oversight regime under the European Supervisory Authorities. It is law, not a certification. A vendor cannot 'be DORA certified.' A financial entity can require contractual clauses, registers of information, and testing cooperation. Oversight of designated critical ICT third-party providers is a public process, not a logo. Typical evidence is contract language and, if the provider is designated, the oversight relationship — not a certificate PDF. ISO 22301 and SOC 2 may support a program; they do not discharge DORA. Weight is moderate as a disclosure claim because it is newly fashionable on trust pages and usually unverified. Regulatory technical standards (RTS/ITS) under DORA fill in registers of information, incident classification, and testing detail. Critical ICT third-party providers are designated; designation is public-ish and rare. Most SaaS vendors are 'ICT third-party providers' to financial entities without being designated critical. The artifact is the contract: access, audit, exit, location, sub-outsourcing. A 'DORA ready' badge is sales language. Threat-led penetration testing duties sit on the financial entity, with cooperation from providers. ISO 22301 and SOC 2 can be exhibits. They are not a DORA certificate because none exists. Score the badge low. Score the contract separately, outside this encyclopedia.

attestations.name: ENS
attestations.issuer: Centro Criptológico Nacional (Spain); certificates by accredited bodies
attestations.eli5: Spain's National Security Scheme for systems that handle government information. Companies get certified at a level: basic, medium, or high. Needed for a lot of Spanish public-sector work.
attestations.elaborate: The Esquema Nacional de Seguridad is Spain's National Security Framework, currently set out in Royal Decree 311/2022. The Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) publishes CCN-STIC guidance. Systems are categorized Básico, Medio, or Alto. Certification is performed by bodies accredited for ENS, not by a blogger and not by ISO automatically. Cloud and SaaS vendors that sell to Spanish public bodies often hold ENS certification for a named service. ENS is not ISO 27001, though 27001 helps. It is not EU-wide. Typical evidence is the ENS certificate stating category and scope. A claim of 'aligned to ENS' without a certificate is a self-statement. Score it as a national government certification, similar in spirit to C5 or SecNumCloud but distinct. CCN-STIC-800 series guides tell you how to interpret ENS for specific technologies. Cloud offerings often certify at Medio; Alto is a different conversation about classification and additional measures. A certificate issued to a reseller is not the SaaS provider's certificate. Spanish public tenders will name the required category. ENS is not EU Cybersecurity Act certification (EUCC / EUCS), which is a different European scheme family. Do not file those here. Typical evidence is the certificate PDF and, where published, a listing. If the vendor says 'ENS aligned' because they have ISO 27001, file that under ISO 27001 and leave this row empty. Score a real Alto or Medio certificate as national public-sector assurance, next to C5 in weight, not next to GDPR.

attestations.name: ePrivacy Directive
attestations.issuer: European Union (Directive 2002/58/EC as amended); implemented by member states
attestations.eli5: An older EU rule about communications privacy and cookies, implemented differently in each country. The proposed ePrivacy Regulation never became the new law. This is not a vendor certificate.
attestations.elaborate: The ePrivacy Directive (2002/58/EC), as amended, is EU law on privacy of electronic communications: traffic data, marketing, and storage of information on a subscriber's device (the 'cookie' rule). Member states implemented it in national law, so the details differ. A proposed ePrivacy Regulation has not replaced it. This is not a certification. Cookie banners and consent tools are not attestations and are out of scope for this register as products. The entry exists so a GRC reader can see why a trust page that says 'ePrivacy compliant' is making a legal claim, not showing an audit. Typical evidence is none as a cert. Weight is low. Do not confuse this with GDPR; they interact, especially on consent and electronic marketing. National implementations include Germany's TTDSG / TDDDG-style rules and similar cookie and communications statutes elsewhere. Direct-marketing calls, PECR in the UK, and app-store tracking prompts all sit in this family of law, not in a certification body's ledger. The failed ePrivacy Regulation is often still mentioned in old policies; it is not in force as a regulation. A consent-management platform is a product, not an attestation, which is why this register refuses to catalog cookie banners. If a vendor lists 'ePrivacy' among certifications, reclassify the string as a legal claim and give it almost no weight. Pair any communications-metadata processing with the GDPR row. That is the clerk's whole job on this one.

attestations.name: EU AI Act
attestations.issuer: European Union (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689); AI Office and national market-surveillance authorities
attestations.eli5: The European Union's law for AI systems, with bans, high-risk duties, and rules for general-purpose models. It is a statute. ISO 42001 is not the same thing.
attestations.elaborate: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the AI Act, is EU law. It uses a risk-based scheme: prohibited practices, high-risk systems with conformity duties, transparency rules, and obligations for general-purpose AI models. Application is phased after entry into force in 2024; do not treat a vendor as 'AI Act certified.' Conformity assessment for high-risk systems, when required, is a regulated product process, not a SOC 2. ISO/IEC 42001 may be used as a management-system input; it is not an EU AI Act certificate. The EU AI Office and national market-surveillance authorities have roles that differ by provision. Typical evidence is none as a cert on a trust page. A GPAI model card or a high-risk technical file, if they exist, are the real artifacts. Weight is low as a claimed badge and high as a legal duty when the product is actually in a regulated class — this register scores the badge. Phased application means some bans and GPAI duties arrive before high-risk product rules. Providers, deployers, importers, and distributors are different roles. A B2B SaaS that lets a customer build high-risk systems may be a provider or a deployer depending on facts; this encyclopedia will not decide that. Conformity assessment, CE marking for high-risk AI, and fundamental-rights impact assessments are regulated processes. None of them is a SOC 2. ISO 42001 may help a management system. It does not produce an AI Act certificate. A 'we comply with the AI Act' badge in 2026 is usually early and unspecific. Ask which role, which system, and which title of the Regulation. Score the badge as a regulation claim.

attestations.name: EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework
attestations.issuer: U.S. Department of Commerce; EU adequacy decision of the European Commission
attestations.eli5: The current EU-to-US transfer list. A US company self-certifies at Commerce and must stay on the public list. It is a transfer tool, not a security audit. Courts have not killed it; people are watching it.
attestations.elaborate: The EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework is a Department of Commerce self-certification program backed by a European Commission adequacy decision (July 2023) for certified organizations. Participants appear on the public Data Privacy Framework List and recertify annually. The UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF is a related UK transfer route; check the listing for which frameworks the organization joined. DPF is not SOC 2 and not a security certification. It addresses whether a US participant's commitments plus US legal safeguards were adequate for EU personal-data transfers. The General Court upheld the adequacy decision in Latombe (appeal status can change). As of August 2026 the adequacy decision remains in force; the EDPB has asked the Commission to review implications of U.S. Supreme Court developments on FTC independence. No court has invalidated DPF. Buyers should open the live list, check the active status and which principles apply, and still prefer SCCs as a fallback. Typical evidence is the listing URL. A logo is not enough. Privacy Shield is not DPF. The listing shows organization name, remaining-in-effect date, and which frameworks (EU-U.S., UK Extension, Swiss-U.S.) are active. An inactive line is not a transfer basis. Supplementary measures and a transfer map are still wise; many counsel run SCCs in parallel. A DPF listing does not attest product security and does not replace a DPA. Recheck the list on the day you sign. Adequacy can end on a court calendar you do not control.

attestations.name: EU-U.S. Privacy Shield
attestations.issuer: U.S. Department of Commerce (invalidated as an EU transfer basis)
attestations.eli5: A dead transfer deal. Europe's top court struck it down in 2020. A company that still says it 'holds Privacy Shield' is showing an expired badge. Do not rely on it.
attestations.elaborate: The EU-U.S. Privacy Shield was a European Commission adequacy arrangement plus a U.S. Department of Commerce self-certification list. The Court of Justice of the European Union invalidated the adequacy decision in Case C-311/18 (Schrems II) on 16 July 2020. The Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield was also discontinued as a transfer basis. Commerce later stood up the Data Privacy Framework, which is a different instrument. Privacy Shield is not a current lawful EU-to-US transfer mechanism. A trust page that still lists it is either historical or wrong. Typical evidence today is none that a buyer should accept. If a vendor cites Privacy Shield, ask for SCCs, BCRs, or a current DPF listing instead. This entry exists so the register can mark the name retired rather than pretend it never existed. Weight is zero for scoring. Commerce stopped treating Privacy Shield as a live EU transfer program after Schrems II. Some organizations left leftover seals on footers for years. Those seals are harmful because they teach buyers the wrong mechanism. Safe Harbor, Privacy Shield's predecessor, was invalidated in Schrems I (2015). The pattern is the point: self-certification adequacy deals with the US have been struck down twice. DPF is the third attempt and is still in force as of this register, with active legal and political watch items. This row's only job is to mark the name retired and to point at DPF, SCCs, and BCRs. Weight is zero. If a crawler sees Privacy Shield, do not add points. Subtract confidence in the page's clerkship.

attestations.name: FedRAMP
attestations.issuer: U.S. General Services Administration, FedRAMP Program Management Office
attestations.eli5: A U.S. government program that checks cloud services before agencies use them. Look the service up on the FedRAMP Marketplace. A blog badge is not an authorization.
attestations.elaborate: The Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program is the U.S. government path for authorizing cloud services that process federal data. Historically, offerings were authorized at FIPS 199 impact levels Low, Moderate, or High, based on NIST SP 800-53 baselines (Rev. 5 is the current baseline family). An independent assessor (3PAO) produces a security assessment package; an agency authorizes use (ATO), and the offering is listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace. The PMO does not 'certify' a company; it lists a cloud service offering. FedRAMP Tailored LI-SaaS is a reduced path for low-impact SaaS and is a separate entry here. In 2026 the program published Consolidated Rules (CR26) that introduce Certification Classes A–D and 'FedRAMP Certified' language; marketplace listings and agency ATOs at Low/Moderate/High remain the labels most buyers still verify. This register does not treat consultant class-mapping blogs as the source of truth — verify the live Marketplace status. FedRAMP is not SOC 2. It is not DoD SRG Impact Level 4/5/6, though packages are reused. Typical evidence is the Marketplace listing for the exact offering name, plus a package under government NDA. 'FedRAMP in process' is not authorized. Weight is high because a real authorization is hard to fake and costly to maintain.
attestations.note: kind uses 'authorization' because that is what agencies and the Marketplace still call a package; CR26 also uses 'certification.' Not a CPA attestation.

attestations.name: FedRAMP Tailored LI-SaaS
attestations.issuer: U.S. General Services Administration, FedRAMP Program Management Office
attestations.eli5: A lighter FedRAMP path for simple, low-impact software in the cloud. It is real. It is not the same as a Moderate or High authorization.
attestations.elaborate: FedRAMP Tailored, Low-Impact Software-as-a-Service (LI-SaaS), is a real FedRAMP policy path for low-risk SaaS where a full Low baseline is disproportionate. The Tailored policy identifies which Low-baseline requirements typically remain on the provider versus the customer or underlying platform, and it uses FedRAMP templates. Authorization is an Agency ATO; there was no JAB P-ATO path for LI-SaaS. The offering should still appear on the FedRAMP Marketplace with the tailored/LI-SaaS designation. It is not Moderate. It is not High. It is not a substitute for DoD IL4. Under CR26, public commentary maps former Low and LI-SaaS toward Certification Class B; buyers should still read the Marketplace line, not a class nickname on a slide. Typical evidence is the Marketplace listing for that offering. A vendor that says 'FedRAMP Tailored' without a listing is making a claim. This entry exists because the user-facing name is common and is not a hybrid invention. Tailored LI-SaaS was built for low-risk tools: collaboration widgets, survey forms, and similar SaaS that do not hold sensitive federal records. If the service will see CUI, Controlled Unclassified Information of higher sensitivity, or Moderate-impact data, LI-SaaS is the wrong row. Agencies can still add controls. Reuse by a second agency is possible after that agency reads the package; it is not automatic. The offering name on the Marketplace must match the offering in the contract. A parent platform's Moderate authorization does not confer LI-SaaS on a different product, or the reverse. Ask for the Marketplace URL and the authorization date. If CR26 class names appear on a slide, map them back to that URL before you score.

attestations.name: FIPS 140-3
attestations.issuer: NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (with Canadian CSEC)
attestations.eli5: A test of a cryptographic module — a library or a hardware box — not of a whole company. Look up the module certificate number. A vendor that says 'we are FIPS certified' is usually stretching.
attestations.elaborate: FIPS 140-3 is the U.S. government standard for cryptographic module security, aligned with ISO/IEC 19790, validated under the NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), jointly with the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security. Certificates attach to a named module and version, at a security level, with a certificate number in the CMVP listing. FIPS 140-2 certificates exist as legacy; new validations are 140-3. This is not a company certification. A SaaS vendor may use a validated module (for example a HSMs or an OpenSSL FIPS provider) inside a service. That does not put the company on the CMVP list. Federal buyers often require validated modules for cryptographic protection of federal data, which is a different demand than FedRAMP, though FedRAMP baselines expect validated cryptography. Typical evidence is the CMVP certificate number and the exact module version used in the product. A trust-page sentence without a number is a claim. Score a verified module listing as specialized crypto evidence, not as an ISMS. Levels 1 through 4 describe increasing physical and physical-security expectations of the module, not the maturity of the vendor's ISMS. Most software libraries land at Level 1; hardware security modules often at Level 3. A certificate can be historical, revoked, or sunset; CMVP states those statuses. 'FIPS validated' and 'FIPS compliant' are different sentences. Compliant often means 'we used algorithms from the approved list' without a module certificate. Federal buyers who require validated modules mean the first sentence. Ask for the certificate number and whether the service runs in FIPS mode (a flag many products expose and some leave off). Score a live CMVP number as crypto-module evidence. Do not score it as company security certification.

attestations.name: GDPR
attestations.issuer: European Union (Regulation (EU) 2016/679); supervised by member-state authorities and the EDPB
attestations.eli5: The European Union's main privacy law. Every company that falls under it must follow it. There is no GDPR certificate. A badge that says 'GDPR certified' is advertising.
attestations.elaborate: The General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679 has applied since 25 May 2018. It is law, not a vendor certification. Supervisory authorities in member states enforce it; the European Data Protection Board coordinates. Controllers and processors that are in scope must meet the Regulation's duties. Article 42 allows certification mechanisms, but there is no single EU-wide 'GDPR certificate' that a SaaS vendor typically holds, and ISO 27701 is not a GDPR certificate. A DPA, a RoPA, SCCs, BCRs, or a DPF listing are tools, not substitutes for the law. A trust-page badge does not move a serious score. This register still includes GDPR because nearly every B2B page claims it, and buyers need a clerk's reminder: ask for the legal mechanism and the DPA, not a logo. Typical evidence of a program — not of 'holding GDPR' — is a DPA, transfer tool, and, if offered, ISO 27701. Weight is low because presence on a page is nearly universal and unverifiable as a cert. Territorial scope (Article 3) catches many non-EU vendors. Mentioning GDPR does not select a lawful basis or appoint a processor. Chapter V transfers still need adequacy or an Article 46 tool. Article 28 contracts are not optional when the vendor is a processor. Enforcement records are public in many member states; a clean trust page can sit next to an ugly decision. This encyclopedia scores the fact that GDPR is a law, not a mark. Do not accept a gold star.

attestations.name: GovRAMP
attestations.issuer: GovRAMP (StateRAMP Inc., d/b/a GovRAMP)
attestations.eli5: A shared cloud-security program for U.S. state and local government, built on NIST 800-53. It used to be called StateRAMP. Check the authorized-products list, not a sticker.
attestations.elaborate: GovRAMP is the current name of the multi-state cloud authorization program that operated as StateRAMP. The rebrand was announced 14 February 2025. StateRAMP Inc. remains the legal entity and operates as GovRAMP; existing memberships and authorizations continued. The program uses NIST SP 800-53-based security status (Ready, Authorized, and program statuses such as Core — verify current status names on govramp.org). It is voluntary at the program level; individual states choose whether and how to require it. It is not FedRAMP. FedRAMP does not automatically grant GovRAMP, or the reverse, though reciprocity conversations exist and Texas TX-RAMP has its own reciprocity rules. Buyers at state agencies should look up the product on the GovRAMP authorized list and confirm the status and impact level. Typical evidence is the public product listing. Older contracts and trust pages will still say StateRAMP; treat that as the same program unless the listing is gone. This is not a CPA attestation. Status names have moved as the program matured (Ready, In Process, Authorized, and program-specific categories). Always read the current authorized-products list rather than a 2023 StateRAMP one-pager. Participating governments decide whether they require GovRAMP or merely recognize it. A city can require something else. Continuous-monitoring duties exist for authorized products; a listing that went stale is not a listing. Reciprocity into TX-RAMP still needs a Texas filing. Reciprocity into FedRAMP is not a right FedRAMP recognizes as automatic. Typical failure mode on a trust page: 'StateRAMP / GovRAMP / FedRAMP aligned' with no product name. Demand the product-level status.

attestations.name: HDS
attestations.issuer: Agence du Numérique en Santé; certificates by COFRAC-accredited bodies
attestations.eli5: A French legal certificate required to host other people's health data. Built on ISO 27001 plus extra health and sovereignty rules. Hospitals in France will ask for it by name.
attestations.elaborate: Hébergeur de Données de Santé is the French certification for hosting personal health data on behalf of others, under the Public Health Code (including article R1111-10 and related decrees). The Agence du Numérique en Santé publishes the certification and accreditation référentiels. Certification bodies accredited by COFRAC (or an equivalent European accreditation body) issue the certificate, typically for three years with surveillance. The scheme requires an ISO/IEC 27001 ISMS covering the hosting activities, plus HDS-specific contract, transparency, and sovereignty requirements. It replaced the older ministerial agrément. It is not HIPAA and not HITRUST. A U.S. HIPAA BAA does not satisfy HDS. Typical evidence is the HDS certificate naming activities and scope. French health buyers will look this up. Score it as a statutory national health-hosting certification. Six activity types appear in the référentiel (from physical hosting through managed platform). The certificate must name which activities were certified. A certificate for physical datacenter housing is not a certificate for a SaaS application layer. HDS v2 référentiels tightened sovereignty language; read the edition on the paper. ISO 27001 is a prerequisite ingredient, not a substitute. SecNumCloud is ANSSI's cloud qualification and is a different, often stricter sovereignty scheme — not merged into this id. A U.S. region of a hyperscaler may be HDS-certified when the hyperscaler completed the process; an ISV on top still needs its own analysis of whether it is 'hosting' under French law. Score a matching HDS certificate high for French health deals.

attestations.name: HIPAA
attestations.issuer: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
attestations.eli5: A U.S. law about health information. There is no official HIPAA certificate. A company can sign a contract and say it follows the rules. That is not the same as a third-party audit.
attestations.elaborate: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, as amended (including HITECH), is U.S. federal law. The Privacy Rule, Security Rule, and Breach Notification Rule are administered by HHS OCR. Covered entities and business associates must comply. There is no HHS-issued 'HIPAA certification.' OCR does not license vendors. A Business Associate Agreement (BAA) is a contract, not an audit. Self-attestation, a security white paper, or a SOC 2 with a HIPAA mapping is not a government approval. HITRUST r2 is often used as a private-sector proxy because the CSF maps HIPAA; it is still not an OCR certificate. 'SOC 2 + HIPAA' is not a separate AICPA product. A buyer should obtain a BAA if required, read whether the vendor will sign one for the product in scope, and treat any third-party report as supporting evidence only. Typical evidence is the BAA plus, if offered, a SOC 2, HITRUST letter, or independent assessment that actually tested Security Rule controls. A trust-page badge that says 'HIPAA compliant' with no BAA and no report is a claim. HIPAA does not apply to all health-adjacent data, and it is not a privacy law for ordinary consumer apps.

attestations.name: HITRUST CSF
attestations.issuer: HITRUST Alliance
attestations.eli5: A big control library that mixes many laws and standards into one set. By itself it is a book of controls, not a certificate. The certificates are e1, i1, and r2.
attestations.elaborate: The HITRUST CSF (also called the HITRUST Framework) is a proprietary control framework maintained by HITRUST Alliance. It maps and tailors requirements from HIPAA, NIST, ISO, PCI, and many other sources into a single catalog. Organizations use it to scope assessments. Holding 'the CSF' is not a certification. The certifiable assessment products built on the CSF are e1, i1, and r2 (and, separately, some targeted or AI-related HITRUST assessments). A vendor that says 'HITRUST CSF certified' without naming e1, i1, or r2 is being vague; ask which assessment and ask for the HITRUST-issued letter. The CSF is threat-adaptive; requirement sets change as HITRUST updates mappings. It is not a government framework, not NIST CSF, and not ISO 27001, though it maps to them. Typical evidence for the framework itself is none — you want the certification letter. This entry exists so a register can distinguish the library from the certificates. Score the letter, not the acronym. HITRUST also publishes threat analyses that change which requirements sit in e1 and i1; that is why those assessments are called threat-adaptive. The CSF is not the NIST Cybersecurity Framework. People shorten both to 'CSF' and then mis-file evidence. If a questionnaire asks 'do you use HITRUST CSF?' the useful answer is which validated assessment you completed, if any. A mapping spreadsheet from an internal GRC tool is not HITRUST-issued. Inheritance from a HITRUST-certified cloud provider can reduce tested requirements; it does not transfer the provider's letter onto you. Keep this row so parsers can attach the framework name without giving it a certificate's weight.

attestations.name: HITRUST e1
attestations.issuer: HITRUST Alliance
attestations.eli5: The smallest HITRUST certificate. An assessor checks a short list of basic security hygiene controls. It lasts one year. It is not the same as the large r2 report hospitals often want.
attestations.elaborate: HITRUST e1 (Essentials, 1-year) is a validated assessment and certification against a fixed set of foundational CSF controls — HITRUST documents this as 43 core controls. A HITRUST Authorized External Assessor performs the validated assessment; HITRUST quality-reviews the file and issues the certification. Validity is one year. e1 is entry-level assurance for lower-risk or less complex organizations. It is not r2, not a HIPAA certificate, and not equivalent to a SOC 2 Type II covering a broad system. Work on e1 can later be reused toward i1. Buyers should read the HITRUST certification letter for the assessed entity, scope, and expiration, and should not accept 'we are HITRUST' without the level. Typical evidence is the HITRUST-issued certification letter, sometimes shared through HITRUST Assessment XChange. A self-assessment against e1 controls without HITRUST certification is not e1. Score e1 below i1 and well below r2. Forty-three controls is a hygiene set, not a hospital-grade specification. e1 does not include the maturity scoring depth of r2. It is a poor substitute when a covered entity's policy says 'HITRUST r2 or equivalent.' Equivalent, in that sentence, usually means r2 or a custom stack, not e1. Read whether optional authoritative sources were added; most e1 letters are the core set only. The assessed legal entity must match the contracting entity. A parent-company e1 does not cover a newly acquired product. If the letter lapsed, there is no grace badge. Ask for the letter, the scope, and the expiration. Then decide whether e1 even answers the question you asked.

attestations.name: HITRUST i1
attestations.issuer: HITRUST Alliance
attestations.eli5: A one-year HITRUST certificate on a larger, fixed set of security practices. Stronger than e1. Not as tailored or deep as r2. Issued by HITRUST after an assessor’s work.
attestations.elaborate: HITRUST i1 (Implemented, 1-year) is a validated assessment against a fixed, threat-adaptive set of CSF controls — HITRUST documents this as 182 controls focused on implemented leading practices. A HITRUST Authorized External Assessor performs the work; HITRUST issues the certification after quality assurance. Validity is one year. i1 is moderate assurance. It is more comprehensive than e1 and less tailored than r2. r2 remains the assessment most large U.S. healthcare delivery organizations still ask for when they want a risk-based, multi-authoritative-source report. i1 is not a government authorization and not a SOC 2. HITRUST describes i1 as a certification with a defined control set and centralized QA, which is a different product shape from a CPA's SOC 2 opinion. Buyers should read the letter, the scope, and whether any optional authoritative sources were added. Typical evidence is the HITRUST certification letter. Work from i1 can be applied toward r2. Do not treat i1 and r2 as interchangeable on a hospital security questionnaire. i1's fixed control set is the point: faster than r2, less argument about scoping, less mapping to every statute. That is also the limit. If a buyer needs a HIPAA, NIST CSF, or FedRAMP mapping baked into a risk-based requirement list, they wanted r2. i1's year-two rapid recertification, when offered, still has to produce a current letter. Do not accept a slide that says 'HITRUST certified' and a verbal 'it's i1.' Get the letter. Compare the assessed entity to the legal name on the order form. i1 is respectable moderate assurance for many SaaS deals outside large health systems. Inside those systems, expect a push to r2.

attestations.name: HITRUST r2
attestations.issuer: HITRUST Alliance
attestations.eli5: The large HITRUST certificate. Controls are picked from the library based on risk and which laws apply. It lasts two years, with a check in the middle. This is the one most hospitals mean.
attestations.elaborate: HITRUST r2 (Risk-based, 2-year) is the highest HITRUST validated assessment commonly seen on U.S. healthcare vendor pages. The requirement set is tailored from the CSF using risk factors such as data volumes, systems, and selected authoritative sources (HIPAA, NIST CSF, and others as scoped). A HITRUST Authorized External Assessor performs the validated assessment; HITRUST issues the certification after quality review. The certification is valid for two years, with a required interim assessment. Domain scoring thresholds apply; r2 is not a participation trophy. It is still not an HHS or OCR certificate. It does not replace a BAA. It does not prove that a specific product module added last month was in the assessed scope. Buyers should read the certification letter, the scope, included authoritative sources, and whether the interim is current. Typical evidence is the HITRUST letter and, under NDA, the full assessment report. r2 is often accepted in place of a stack of smaller questionnaires; that is a buyer policy choice, not a law. e1 and i1 are different products. r2 reports are long. The useful pages are the scope, the risk-factor questionnaire that selected requirements, the domain scores, and any corrective-action items. A certificate letter without the report is enough to prove the mark exists; it is not enough to see what was weak. Interim assessments can fail or add conditions; ask if the interim is done and whether the letter is still valid. Authoritative-source coverage is chosen, not automatic — a letter that did not include HIPAA is a poor HIPAA proxy. HITRUST QA is real and is why buyers treat r2 as stronger than a lone SOC 2 mapping. Not OCR.

attestations.name: IRAP
attestations.issuer: Australian Signals Directorate (assessors); consuming agency accepts the assessment
attestations.eli5: Australia's program of registered assessors who check systems against the government's information-security manual. ASD does not hand you a consumer certificate. An agency decides whether to accept the report.
attestations.elaborate: The Information Security Registered Assessors Program is run by the Australian Signals Directorate. IRAP assessors independently assess systems against the Australian Government Information Security Manual (ISM) and related guidance. ASD endorses assessors; it does not issue a public 'IRAP certified' consumer mark for a SaaS brand. A consuming Australian government agency decides whether to accept the assessment for a classification (commonly Official or Protected for commercial cloud). Typical evidence is an IRAP assessment report and the agency's acceptance, plus any ASD or buyer listing of assessed services. Cloud hyperscalers publish which regions and services have been IRAP-assessed. A marketing line 'IRAP certified' without a classification, assessor, and service list is overstated. IRAP is not FedRAMP. It is not Essential Eight certification — Essential Eight is a different ASD maturity model. Score a documented Protected assessment high for Australian public sector. Classifications you will actually see on commercial cloud are Official and Protected. Secret and above are a different hosting world. ASD publishes guidance and the ISM; the consumer agency still owns the risk acceptance. Hyperscalers list IRAP-assessed services per region; an ISV on top needs its own story. Essential Eight maturity is a separate ASD model often asked in the same breath; it is not IRAP. A consultant 'IRAP-aligned' workshop is not an assessment. Ask for the assessor's name (they are on the ASD endorsed list), the classification, the date, and which services. Score a current Protected assessment in the same band as other national cloud authorizations. Score a slide deck as zero.

attestations.name: ISMAP
attestations.issuer: ISMAP Steering Committee (Digital Agency / METI / MIC / NISC)
attestations.eli5: Japan's government cloud-security register. A cloud service is audited and then listed if it passes. If it is not on the list, it is not ISMAP.
attestations.elaborate: The Information system Security Management and Assessment Program is Japan's government program for assessing cloud services used in government information systems. The ISMAP Steering Committee (Digital Agency, METI, MIC, NISC and related bodies) governs it. Registered audit organizations assess services against the ISMAP control set; successful services appear on the ISMAP Cloud Service List. There is also ISMAP-LIU for lower-impact use, which is a lighter listing — read which list the service is on. ISMAP is not ISO 27001, though 27001 is typically part of the evidence pile. It is not FedRAMP. Typical evidence is the service's presence on the official ISMAP list, with the registered date and scope. A Japanese-language 'ISMAP aligned' slide is not a listing. Score a live listing as a national government cloud authorization. The official list is the only source of truth. Japanese-government procurement of public cloud has increasingly pointed at ISMAP-registered services. ISMAP-LIU exists for lower-impact use and must not be sold as full ISMAP. Audit bodies are registered; a random ISO auditor is not automatically an ISMAP auditor. Listings expire and must be maintained. A global ISO 27001 on a US entity does not put a Tokyo region on the ISMAP list. Ask for the list URL and the service name in Japanese and English if both exist. Score a live full listing high for Japanese public-sector deals. Score 'planning to apply' as nothing. This is Japan's FedRAMP-shaped object, not Japan's PDPA.
attestations.note: ISMAP-LIU is a related lighter listing; confirm on the official list rather than treating it as full ISMAP.

attestations.name: ISO 13485
attestations.issuer: ISO; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A quality-system certificate for medical-device companies. It is about how devices are designed and made, not about a hospital SaaS being HIPAA certified.
attestations.elaborate: ISO 13485:2016 is the quality management system standard for medical devices and related services. An accredited certification body (often also a regulatory notified-body or MDSAP participant, depending on market) certifies that the named scope runs a device QMS: design control, risk, supplier control, traceability, complaint handling, and documented manufacturing. It is relevant when the vendor is a device manufacturer or a software-as-a-medical-device organization. It is not HIPAA, not HITRUST, and not ISO 27001. A digital health SaaS that is not a device may hold 27001 and not 13485; that can be correct. Conversely, 13485 without a security attestation is a weak answer to a hospital security questionnaire. It does not prove clinical safety of a specific device version, and it is not an FDA 510(k) or CE mark under the EU MDR/IVDR. Buyers should read the scope (which devices or software) and the regulatory scheme the QMS supports. Typical evidence is the certificate. Include this in a security encyclopedia because health-tech vendors routinely list it next to security marks; it is a quality mark, scored as such. Software as a medical device organizations use 13485 alongside IEC 62304 and, in the EU, MDR/IVDR conformity. A wellness SaaS that is not a device should not hide behind 13485. A device maker with 13485 and no 27001 still owes a security story if the device phones home. Read the device list on the certificate. Typical buyer mistake is treating 13485 as HIPAA. It is not. Keep the row because health-tech pages list it next to SOC 2, and a clerk has to un-mix them.

attestations.name: ISO 22301
attestations.issuer: ISO; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A certificate that the company has a business-continuity system: plans for when things break, and practice at those plans. It is not a backup screenshot and not an uptime SLA.
attestations.elaborate: ISO 22301:2019 is the certifiable business continuity management system (BCMS) standard. An accredited certification body audits whether the organization identifies continuity requirements, runs impact analysis, sets strategies, and exercises plans for a stated scope. The certificate attests the management system, not a particular recovery-time objective on your tenant. It does not replace the contractual SLA, disaster-recovery runbooks, or a SOC 2 availability category. It does not prove the last exercise restored the product you buy. Buyers should read the scope (which services and sites), ask for exercise frequency and last exercise date under NDA, and match RTO/RPO to the contract. Typical evidence is the certificate. Some vendors offer a SOC 2 with availability instead of, or in addition to, 22301. Both can be valid; they are different artifacts. ISO 22301 is not cyber-resilience regulation. EU financial entities under DORA have statutory resilience duties that a 22301 certificate may support but does not discharge. A BCMS certificate should rest on a business-impact analysis that names recovery objectives. Those numbers belong in the contract, not only in the ISMS. Ask whether the last exercise was a tabletop or a full restore, which product was restored, and whether the restore met the documented RTO. Cloud customers often discover that the certified BCMS covers the provider's office network and not the multi-tenant production service. That gap is common and is why scope language matters. 22301 does not prove ransomware readiness by itself. It does not replace cyber-insurance questionnaires or DORA ICT-testing duties for financial entities. If the vendor also has SOC 2 availability, read both; they test different claims. Expired 22301 is just a plan on a shelf.

attestations.name: ISO 9001
attestations.issuer: ISO; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A quality-management certificate. It says the company has a system for consistent work and complaints, not that its software is secure. Common, and easy to over-read.
attestations.elaborate: ISO 9001:2015 is the generic quality management system (QMS) standard. An accredited certification body issues a certificate that the named scope runs a QMS meeting 9001 requirements: customer focus, documented processes, corrective action, and improvement. It is not an information-security, privacy, or AI certificate. It does not attest software security, uptime, or lawful processing. Many manufacturers, device makers, and professional-services firms hold it. Software vendors sometimes display it because it is familiar to procurement. A buyer running a security review should not score ISO 9001 as if it were ISO 27001. For medical devices, ISO 13485 is the more specific QMS and should be preferred when that is the industry. Read the scope and expiry. Typical evidence is the certificate. Combined 9001/27001 certificates exist; read each scope. This register gives it a low public-disclosure weight because it is widely held and weakly related to security claims on a trust page. Procurement teams like 9001 because it is familiar from manufacturing tenders. That is also why it shows up on software trust pages that have no security certificate yet. The standard says almost nothing about access control, encryption, logging, or vulnerability management. A nonconformity on document control is not a security finding. If the same certification body issued 9001 and 27001, still read two scopes; they are often different legal entities. The 2015 edition remains the current certifiable edition as of this register. A company can lose 9001 and still have a fine ISMS, and the reverse. Do not let 9001 move a security score more than a point or two. If you are buying a medical device, stop reading this row and open ISO 13485.

attestations.name: ISO/IEC 20000-1
attestations.issuer: ISO/IEC; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A certificate that the company manages IT services in a formal way — incidents, changes, service levels. It is not a security audit of the product.
attestations.elaborate: ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018 is the certifiable IT service management system (SMS) standard. An accredited certification body audits whether the organization plans, designs, delivers, and improves services under a documented SMS for a stated scope. The family is related to ITIL practice but the certificate is to the ISO standard, not to AXELOS/PeopleCert ITIL training. It attests service-management process, not the security of a cloud control plane. It does not replace ISO 27001 or SOC 2. Some public-sector and outsourcing tenders still ask for it. Buyers should read the scope for which services are covered and not infer security testing from a 20000-1 logo. Typical evidence is the certificate. French HDS certification historically leaned on ISO 27001 and, for some activities, service-management evidence; HDS is a separate legal certification. ISO 20000-1 is not a continuity certificate (see 22301) and not a quality certificate (see 9001). Service-management certificates are still written into some government and outsourcing frameworks, especially where the buyer grew up on ITIL. The useful questions are: which services, which service desk, which change advisory board, and whether production incidents on your product would even enter that SMS. A 20000-1 certificate on a professional-services unit does not cover the SaaS. It does not attest vulnerability SLAs or encryption. Overlap with ISO 27001 is organizational, not technical. If a French hosting deal mentions both 20000-1 and HDS, HDS is the legal one for health data; 20000-1 is supporting. Ask for the certificate scope page. A pink ITIL training card on an employee's wall is not this certificate.

attestations.name: ISO/IEC 27001
attestations.issuer: ISO/IEC; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A third party checked that the company runs an information-security management system and keeps improving it. The certificate names a scope. If your product is outside that scope, the paper does not cover you.
attestations.elaborate: ISO/IEC 27001 is the certifiable information security management system (ISMS) standard. The current edition is ISO/IEC 27001:2022. An accredited certification body, not ISO itself, audits and issues a three-year certificate with annual surveillance. The certificate attests that the named organization operates an ISMS for a stated scope — legal entities, locations, and services. It does not attest that a particular SaaS tenant cannot be breached, that every control in Annex A is implemented everywhere, or that personal data is processed lawfully. Annex A is a reference control set; Statement of Applicability decisions matter. Buyers should read the certificate scope, the certification body and accreditation mark (for example UKAS, ANAB, DAkkS), the expiry date, and whether the edition is 2022. A 2013 certificate after the transition window is stale. ISO 27001 is not SOC 2, not FedRAMP, and not a privacy law. It pairs often with ISO 27017 and 27018 for cloud, and with ISO 27701 for privacy. Typical evidence is the certificate PDF plus, under NDA, the statement of applicability or a high-level SoA extract. A 'certified' claim without a scope line is incomplete. Surveillance and recertification dates belong in the file.

attestations.name: ISO/IEC 27017
attestations.issuer: ISO/IEC; typically certified as an extension by an accredited body
attestations.eli5: Extra cloud-security guidance that sits on top of ISO 27001. It says how a cloud provider and a cloud customer should split the work. It is not a stand-alone gold star.
attestations.elaborate: ISO/IEC 27017 is a code of practice giving cloud-specific guidance on ISO/IEC 27002 controls, plus additional cloud controls, for both cloud service providers and cloud customers. The commonly cited edition is ISO/IEC 27017:2015. Organizations usually obtain it as an extension to an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate, not as a free-standing management-system certification. It addresses shared responsibility, virtualization, admin rights, customer isolation, and alignment of cloud roles. It does not replace ISO 27001. It does not attest privacy of personal data in the public cloud; that is closer to ISO 27018. It is not CSA STAR, though the topics overlap with the Cloud Controls Matrix. A buyer should confirm the 27017 mark appears on the certificate or in the certification body's scope language, and that the cloud service in the deal is inside that scope. Typical evidence is the ISO 27001 certificate listing 27017, or a separate statement from the certification body. A blog sentence that the company 'follows 27017' without a certificate is a practice claim, not a certification. Combined 27001/27017/27018 certificates are common at large cloud providers. Certification bodies differ in how they print the extension. Ask for the page that names 27017. Shared-responsibility tables in the SoA are the useful part; customer-owned controls marked 'not applicable' without saying they are yours is sloppy scoping. 27017 does not replace CSA STAR Level 2 and does not speak to model risk. Surveillance should keep 27017 in scope each year. If the 27001 certificate expired, the extension expired with it.

attestations.name: ISO/IEC 27018
attestations.issuer: ISO/IEC; typically certified as an extension by an accredited body
attestations.eli5: Cloud privacy guidance for companies that hold other people's personal data in a public cloud. It rides along with ISO 27001. It is not GDPR and it is not a government permit.
attestations.elaborate: ISO/IEC 27018 is a code of practice for protecting personally identifiable information (PII) in public clouds acting as PII processors. The commonly cited edition is ISO/IEC 27018:2019. Like 27017, it is usually certified as an extension to ISO/IEC 27001 rather than as its own ISMS. It adds processor-oriented controls: purpose limitation, return and deletion of PII, transparency to the customer, and restrictions on use of customer data for provider marketing. It does not make the provider a GDPR-compliant controller. It does not replace a data processing agreement, SCCs, or a transfer mechanism. It does not cover every privacy law. A company that is a controller, or that processes PII only in a private cloud, may be outside the intended use. Buyers should check that the certificate scope names the cloud service and the processor role, and should still execute a DPA. Typical evidence is the ISO 27001 certificate listing 27018. ISO 27701 is the broader privacy information management system and is the better artifact if you need a PIMS, not only public-cloud processor guidance. Read whether the certified role is processor only. Deletion and return commitments still have to appear in the DPA you sign. Sub-processors are in scope only if the SoA says so. 27018 is silent on U.S. state statutes and on HIPAA. Do not let a 27018 logo stand in for a BAA, an SCC module, or a transfer impact assessment. Pair with 27701 when you need a full PIMS.

attestations.name: ISO/IEC 27701
attestations.issuer: ISO/IEC; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A certificate that the company runs a privacy management system for personal data. The 2019 version hung off ISO 27001. The 2025 version can stand alone. It is not a GDPR certificate from the EU.
attestations.elaborate: ISO/IEC 27701 specifies a privacy information management system (PIMS) for PII controllers and processors. ISO/IEC 27701:2019 was written as an extension to ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002; most certificates you will still see are 2019 extensions on a 27001 ISMS. ISO/IEC 27701:2025, published 14 October 2025, is a standalone PIMS standard. Transition rules for existing 2019 certificates are set by accreditation and certification bodies; do not assume a date that is not on the paper. The certificate attests that the named scope operates a PIMS. It does not attest legal compliance with GDPR, CPRA, LGPD, or any other statute, and it is not issued by a data-protection authority. It does not replace records of processing, DPIAs, or transfer tools. Buyers should read the scope, whether the organization is certified as controller, processor, or both, the edition year, and the certification body's accreditation. Typical evidence is the certificate PDF. A 'GDPR certified' claim citing only 27701 is overstated. Pair it with the actual transfer mechanism (SCCs, DPF, BCRs) and the DPA. ISO 27018 remains the narrower public-cloud processor code of practice. Until your certification body prints 2025 on the paper, you are looking at the 2019 extension. Ask which processing activities were in scope, whether employees and customers were both covered, and whether subprocessors were included. 27701 does not approve BCRs and does not replace a DPO appointment where law requires one. Treat it as management-system evidence next to the legal tools, not as a substitute.

attestations.name: ISO/IEC 42001
attestations.issuer: ISO/IEC; certificate issued by an accredited certification body
attestations.eli5: A certificate that the company has a management system for building and using AI on purpose, with roles, risk steps, and reviews. It does not prove a model is fair or safe in your case.
attestations.elaborate: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is the certifiable artificial intelligence management system (AIMS) standard. An accredited certification body audits whether the organization has established, implemented, and continually improved an AIMS for a stated scope: AI systems developed, provided, or used. The standard covers AI policy, risk, impact assessment, data for AI systems, lifecycle controls, and supplier relationships. It is not a model card, not a red-team report, and not an EU AI Act conformity assessment. It does not prove a given model is accurate, unbiased, or lawful to deploy in a high-risk use. The EU AI Act is a regulation; 42001 is a voluntary management-system certificate that some organizations use as supporting evidence. 'SOC 2 Type II AI' is not an ISO or AICPA product; if a vendor uses that phrase, ask for the ordinary SOC 2 plus this certificate or a scoped description, not a hybrid brand. Buyers should read the certificate scope (which products, which models, which business units), the certification body, and the expiry. Typical evidence is the certificate PDF. Absence of 42001 is not evidence the vendor has no AI program; presence is not evidence your use case was assessed.

attestations.name: K-ISMS
attestations.issuer: Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) / Ministry of Science and ICT
attestations.eli5: South Korea's information-security management certification. Required for a lot of Korean public and large-service work. Related to ISO 27001 but it is a Korean legal scheme.
attestations.elaborate: K-ISMS is the Korean Information Security Management System certification operated with KISA under Korean law (the Information and Communications Network Act framework and related rules). It certifies that an organization operates an ISMS meeting the Korean control set. It is influenced by ISO/IEC 27001 but is not the same certificate. Korea also operates a cloud-specific scheme (often referred to in English as CSAP / cloud security assurance) that is distinct; do not merge them. Typical evidence is the K-ISMS certificate issued in the Korean program, with scope and validity. A global ISO 27001 certificate is not K-ISMS. Score K-ISMS as a national ISMS certification when the buyer is Korean public sector or a regulated Korean service. Korean public and large internet services have statutory or practical K-ISMS duties that do not apply to a random global SaaS. If the customer is not Korean, this row rarely matters. If the customer is a Korean government cloud buyer, they may also mention CSAP (cloud security assurance). CSAP is not filed under this id. Certificates are in Korean; get a translation of the scope, not only a logo. ISO 27001 can be used as input but the K-ISMS certificate is the object. Score it when present and in scope. Do not treat a global 27001 as a substitute for a Korean buyer who asked for K-ISMS by name. That substitution is a common trust-page hope and a common failed questionnaire answer.
attestations.note: Korea's cloud CSAP is a separate scheme; not merged into this entry.

attestations.name: LGPD
attestations.issuer: Brazil (Lei nº 13.709/2018); Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados
attestations.eli5: Brazil's general data-protection law. The national authority is the ANPD. It is a law, not a certificate a vendor can buy.
attestations.elaborate: The Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados Pessoais (Law 13.709/2018) is Brazil's general data-protection statute. The Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados (ANPD) is the supervisor. It is not a certification. Agent roles (controller/operator) and transfer tools are legal constructs.
