A 'LGPD compliant' badge is a claim. Typical evidence is a Brazilian-law DPA and, if used, a transfer mechanism recognized under the statute. Weight is low. Do not treat ISO 27701 as an ANPD certificate. LGPD has lawful bases, DPO-style roles (encarregado), international-transfer rules, and ANPD guidance that has been catching up since the authority stood up. Some transfer regulations and adequacy-style decisions may exist or be in progress; do not invent an ANPD vendor certificate. Brazil also has sector rules (for example in finance and health) that sit beside LGPD. A 'LGPD seal' sold by a consultant is not ANPD. ISO 27701 can support a program. The contract still has to pick Brazilian law when that is the deal. Score the statute low. If a trust page lists LGPD next to SOC 2 as if they were the same kind of object, the page is mixed up. This row exists to un-mix it and to give the clerk enough words to say so without inventing a Brazilian certification scheme that the ANPD does not run for SaaS vendors.

attestations.name: MTCS
attestations.issuer: IMDA Singapore (SS 584); certified by accredited bodies
attestations.eli5: Singapore's multi-tier cloud security standard. Providers get certified at Level 1, 2, or 3. Level 3 is the strictest. It is a real certificate, not just the PDPA law.
attestations.elaborate: The Multi-Tier Cloud Security standard is Singapore Standard SS 584, under the Infocomm Media Development Authority. Certification bodies audit cloud providers to one of three tiers (Level 1 baseline through Level 3). The certificate names the service and the level. MTCS is not the PDPA. It is not CSA STAR, though topics overlap. Typical evidence is the MTCS certificate and any IMDA or certification-body listing. Read the level and the service name. A Level 1 certificate is not Level 3. Score it as a national cloud certification, below IRAP/FedRAMP in this register because the buyer population is narrower, but it is independent assurance. SS 584 tiers are cumulative in spirit: a Level 3 service has met a stricter set than Level 1. Public sector and regulated buyers in Singapore may name a tier. The certificate is issued by an accredited certification body, not by a blog. Scope can be IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS; read it. MTCS is sometimes discussed next to Singapore's Cyber Trust marks; those are different CSA Singapore schemes. PDPA remains the privacy law. A vendor that holds MTCS Level 2 and ISO 27001 is showing two real marks. A vendor that holds neither and writes 'aligned to MTCS' is mapping. Score the certificate at the stated level. If the level is missing, ask. Do not guess Level 3.

attestations.name: NIS2
attestations.issuer: European Union (Directive (EU) 2022/2555); implemented by member states
attestations.eli5: An EU directive that makes more essential and important entities, and some of their suppliers, meet cybersecurity duties. Each country writes it into national law. Not a certificate.
attestations.elaborate: The NIS2 Directive (EU) 2022/2555 replaces the first NIS Directive and expands the set of essential and important entities. Member states transpose it into national law; the transposition deadline was 17 October 2024, and national implementations differ. It is not a vendor certification. There is no 'NIS2 certificate' issued by the Commission. Some countries overlay national schemes (for example, existing essential-service security laws). A SaaS vendor may be in scope as an important entity or as a supplier that gets contractual flow-down. Typical evidence is none as a cert. A trust-page badge is a claim. Pair with national schemes (C5, ENS, Cyber Essentials) when those are the actual artifacts. Weight is low. Essential and important entities are defined by sector annexes and size tests in national law. Management accountability, incident reporting, and supply-chain security are the headline duties. A SaaS vendor may be in scope as a digital provider or only as a supplier. Member-state registers and competent authorities differ. There is talk of certification schemes under the Cybersecurity Act helping with NIS2; that is not a NIS2 certificate and not this row. A trust page that lists NIS2 next to ISO 27001 as two certificates is wrong. File NIS2 as regulation. If the vendor has C5, ENS, or Cyber Essentials, those are the national artifacts that might actually sit on disk.

attestations.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
attestations.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
attestations.eli5: A NIST guidebook for managing risks of AI systems. Companies can follow it. NIST does not certify that they did. It is not the EU AI Act.
attestations.elaborate: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0, NIST AI 100-1, January 2023) is voluntary guidance for governing, mapping, measuring, and managing risks of AI systems. A companion playbook exists. NIST does not issue AI RMF certificates. A vendor claim of 'NIST AI RMF aligned' is a self-description unless an independent assessor mapped practices to the Core and documented evidence. It is not ISO/IEC 42001, which is a certifiable AIMS. It is not the EU AI Act. Buyers who need AI assurance should prefer a scoped ISO 42001 certificate, a system card with evaluation results, and contractual terms, and should treat AI RMF as the vocabulary, not the proof. Typical evidence is a public mapping or an assessment report, not a NIST logo. Score it like other voluntary frameworks. AI 100-1 is organized around Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. The playbook is a companion, not a second standard. Sector profiles (for example for generative AI) may exist as NIST publications; they are still guidance. Independent assessors can use the RMF as criteria, but unless you hold that report you have a blog post. ISO 42001 is the certifiable cousin. The EU AI Act is the legal cousin. A model-card PDF is closer to useful evidence than an 'AI RMF aligned' badge. Score the framework only. If a vendor has 42001, score that row and treat this one as vocabulary.

attestations.name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
attestations.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
attestations.eli5: A popular way to organize cybersecurity work: identify, protect, detect, respond, recover — and now govern. Anyone can say they use it. NIST does not hand out CSF certificates.
attestations.elaborate: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is voluntary guidance. CSF 2.0 was published in February 2024 and adds a Govern function to Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Organizations adopt it as a language for programs and assessments. NIST does not certify companies to the CSF. HITRUST can produce a NIST CSF scorecard from a HITRUST assessment; that is a HITRUST product, not a NIST certificate. A SOC 2 or ISO 27001 can be mapped to CSF functions; the mapping is not a CSF certification. Buyers should treat 'aligned to NIST CSF' as a narrative unless an independent report maps controls to the Core. Typical evidence is that mapping or a HITRUST CSF scorecard, not a NIST seal. This framework is widely claimed and weakly evidentiary, so it scores low as a public-disclosure mover. CSF 2.0 profiles and implementation examples are guidance. Some regulators and insurers ask for a CSF self-tier (Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive under the older Tiers). That self-tier is not an audit. HITRUST's NIST CSF scorecard, when present, is the rare third-party-looking artifact and still comes from HITRUST, not NIST. Mapping SOC 2 TSC to CSF functions is a slide exercise. This register keeps the row because the string appears on almost every mature trust page. It should barely move a score. If you need assurance, open the SOC 2, the ISO certificate, or the HITRUST letter instead.

attestations.name: NIST SP 800-171
attestations.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
attestations.eli5: The NIST control set for protecting controlled unclassified information on a contractor's own systems. Defense contracts have pointed at Revision 2. It is not a certificate by itself.
attestations.elaborate: NIST SP 800-171, Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations, specifies security requirements for CUI on contractor systems. Revision 2 is the version CMMC Level 2 and DFARS 252.204-7012 currently use. Revision 3 has been published; do not assume a contract moved to Rev. 3 unless the contract says so. There is no NIST 800-171 certificate. Contractors self-assess and post scores to SPRS; some obtain a CMMC Level 2 C3PAO assessment against the same 110 requirements. A '800-171 compliant' badge on a trust page is a claim. Typical evidence is the SPRS score date, a system security plan, and, if offered, a CMMC status. 800-171 is not 800-53 and not FedRAMP. It does not apply merely because a SaaS vendor sells to a company that has a defense contract — it applies when CUI is processed on the vendor's system and the flow-down says so. DFARS 252.204-7012 still points at 800-171 Rev. 2 and at incident-reporting clocks that have nothing to do with a trust-page badge. SPRS scores are out of 110 with deductions; a score of 104 with open POA&Ms is not 'compliant' in the casual sense. CMMC Level 2 uses the same 110 requirements but is a different status language. 800-172 enhanced requirements are not this row. A SaaS vendor processing CUI becomes part of the contractor's environment; flow-down should be in the contract, not inferred from a logo. Ask for the system boundary, the SPRS date, and whether any CUI lands in the commercial multi-tenant cloud.

attestations.name: NIST SP 800-53
attestations.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
attestations.eli5: A large U.S. government catalog of security and privacy controls. Agencies and FedRAMP use it. A company cannot be '800-53 certified.' It can be assessed against a baseline.
attestations.elaborate: NIST Special Publication 800-53 is the Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations catalog. Revision 5 is the current revision used with FedRAMP baselines. It is a control catalog, not a certification program. There is no NIST-issued 800-53 certificate. FedRAMP, GovRAMP, TX-RAMP, and many agency authorizations select baselines (Low/Moderate/High, or program-specific) from this catalog. A vendor claim of 'NIST 800-53 compliant' without a baseline, an assessor, and a package is a self-assertion. Buyers should ask which revision, which baseline, who assessed it, and whether the result is a FedRAMP package, a GovRAMP status, or an internal mapping. Typical evidence is the authorization listing or an assessment report, not the SP itself. 800-53 is not 800-171. 800-171 is a derived set for nonfederal systems that process CUI. Do not score a 800-53 poster as equal to FedRAMP. Revision 5 reorganized privacy controls into the main catalog and changed control families. A mapping written to Rev. 4 is a different object. Baselines are published as 800-53B. Overlaying a custom set and calling it '800-53' without saying Moderate or High is how vendors hide a short control list. FedRAMP baselines add and parameterize controls; they are not vanilla 800-53. DoD SRG overlays are different again. If the only artifact is an internal spreadsheet, score this as a framework claim. If the artifact is a FedRAMP Moderate package, score FedRAMP, not this row. NIST does not sell a plaque.

attestations.name: PCI 3DS
attestations.issuer: PCI Security Standards Council
attestations.eli5: A PCI standard for the computers that run 3-D Secure, the extra card-check step at checkout. It is not the same as being PCI DSS compliant for a shop.
attestations.elaborate: PCI 3DS refers to the PCI 3-D Secure Core Security Standard and related assessment program for environments that operate EMV 3-D Secure components: 3DS Servers, Directory Servers, and Access Control Servers. The PCI Security Standards Council publishes the standard. Assessors qualified for the 3DS program test those environments. Payment brands decide who must validate. This is not PCI DSS, though a 3DS environment may also be in a DSS scope. It is not a merchant 'we use 3-D Secure' badge. A checkout that offers 3-D Secure through a processor does not make the merchant PCI 3DS validated. Typical evidence is a 3DS Attestation of Compliance or listing appropriate to the role. Buyers of 3DS vendor platforms should ask which component was assessed and against which version. Do not treat a PCI DSS AOC as proof of 3DS, or the reverse. The program exists because 3-D Secure systems handle authentication data and protocol security that DSS alone does not fully cover. EMV 3-D Secure is a protocol. PCI 3DS is the security standard for the parties that operate its core components. Issuers, directory-server operators, and 3DS-server vendors are the usual assessed entities. A merchant that 'turned on 3DS' through an acquirer has not been assessed to PCI 3DS. Confusion with PCI DSS requirement 3 and with 3DS as a fraud-reduction feature is common on trust pages. Ask for the component type, the assessor, and the AOC date. If the company is only a merchant, this row should not appear. If the company sells a 3DS server, the listing should match the product version you would run. This is payments infrastructure assurance, scored below DSS because fewer buyers need it.

attestations.name: PCI DSS
attestations.issuer: PCI Security Standards Council; validated by a QSA or via SAQ
attestations.eli5: Rules for companies that store, process, or transmit payment-card data. A qualified assessor or a self-questionnaire checks them. It is about cardholder data, not general privacy.
attestations.elaborate: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard is issued by the PCI Security Standards Council. Current published versions are PCI DSS 4.0 and 4.0.1; 3.2.1 is retired. Payment brands (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, JCB) decide who must validate and how. Level 1 service providers and many large merchants require an annual Report on Compliance (ROC) by a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) plus an Attestation of Compliance (AOC). Smaller entities may use a Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) of the matching type. The standard protects cardholder data and sensitive authentication data. It does not attest general corporate security, HIPAA, or SOC 2. A company can be PCI compliant for a payment environment and weak elsewhere. Scope reduction via a payment processor or P2PE matters; read the AOC for what was in scope. 'PCI certified' is loose talk. Typical evidence is the AOC (often shareable) and, under NDA, the ROC. Check the version, the QSA, the date, and whether the company is a merchant or a service provider. PCI DSS is not PCI 3DS and not the Software Security Framework. If the AOC still says 3.2.1 after retirement, it is stale. Service-provider AOCs are not merchant AOCs. Ask whether the company stores account data or uses a redirect/iframe model that shrinks scope. Quarterly ASV scans and penetration tests are part of the standard; a year-old AOC does not prove last quarter's scan passed. Get the AOC. Decline a logo.

attestations.name: PCI Software Security Framework
attestations.issuer: PCI Security Standards Council
attestations.eli5: PCI's modern program for payment software and for how that software is built. It replaced the old PA-DSS listing for payment applications. Two standards sit inside it.
attestations.elaborate: The PCI Software Security Framework (SSF) is the PCI SSC's program for payment software security. It contains two standards. The Secure Software Standard is used to validate specific payment software products; successful products are listed as Validated Payment Software. The Secure Software Lifecycle (Secure SLC) Standard is used to validate a vendor's secure development and maintenance process; successful vendors are listed as Secure SLC Qualified Vendors. SSF Assessor Companies, qualified by PCI SSC, perform the assessments. SSF succeeds PA-DSS for payment applications; PA-DSS is retired and should not be claimed as current. SSF is not PCI DSS. A merchant's DSS AOC does not list software. A software vendor can hold SSF listings and still need DSS if it also stores card data as a service provider. Typical evidence is the PCI SSC public listing plus the report on validation where shareable. Read which standard, which product version, and the expiry. 'PCI certified software' without a listing URL is incomplete. PA-DSS listings sunset on a PCI SSC timetable; do not accept a PA-DSS letter as current for new software. Secure Software validation is product-version specific — a new major release is a new listing. Secure SLC qualification is about the vendor's lifecycle and can allow certain delta self-attestations for already listed software; it is not a blanket license to skip product validation. Read the PCI SSC list, not a PDF the vendor designed. SSF assessors are not the same roster as QSAs, though some firms are both. SSF does not replace DSS for a service provider that stores PAN. It does not speak to ISO 42001 or application security of a non-payment product in the same company. Two listings, two questions.

attestations.name: PDPA (Singapore)
attestations.issuer: Singapore; Personal Data Protection Commission
attestations.eli5: Singapore's personal-data law, enforced by the PDPC. Not the same law as Thailand's PDPA. Not a certificate.
attestations.elaborate: Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act is national law, administered by the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC). It is not Thailand's PDPA and not Malaysia's PDPA. It is not a certification, though Singapore also has other cyber marks (for example Cyber Trust / Cyber Essentials-style marks under CSA Singapore) that are separate from the statute. A vendor cannot hold PDPA. Typical evidence is a Singapore-law processing agreement and a PDPC-aligned notice. Weight is low. MTCS is the Singapore cloud security standard and is a different entry. PDPC issues advisory guidelines (including for cloud and for AI in later years) and can fine. It does not certify B2B software. Singapore's Cyber Security Agency has separate cyber labelling schemes; those are not the PDPA. Do not file a Cyber Trust Mark under this id. Do not file MTCS under this id. A transfer out of Singapore uses PDPA transfer tools, not EU SCCs unless the contract also needs EU law. The acronym collision with Thailand is the main catalog risk. Always write 'PDPA (Singapore).' Weight is low. Typical evidence is a PDPA schedule in the DPA naming the PDPC as the relevant authority. A badge that says PDPA without a flag is defective data and should not increment a score.

attestations.name: PDPA (Thailand)
attestations.issuer: Thailand; Office of the Personal Data Protection Committee
attestations.eli5: Thailand's personal-data law. Same acronym as Singapore's, different country and different statute. Still not a certificate.
attestations.elaborate: Thailand's Personal Data Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) is national law. The Office of the Personal Data Protection Committee (PDPC) is the supervisor. It shares an English acronym with Singapore's PDPA and must not be merged with it. It is not a certification. A trust page that says 'PDPA' without a country is ambiguous. Typical evidence is a Thailand-law processing agreement. Weight is low. This entry exists so the register does not collapse two statutes. Thailand's PDPA came into full enforcement on a published timetable after delays; the Office of the PDPC issues notifications that change operational detail. Extra-territorial reach can catch foreign vendors that target Thai persons. There is no Thai PDPA certificate for a global SaaS. Cross-border transfer rules and a secretary-general approval path exist in the statute and notifications — read the current notification, do not rely on this paragraph as a transfer memo. Keep the row so 'PDPA' on a Bangkok customer's questionnaire does not get filed under Singapore. Score it as a regulation. If a vendor claims a Thai privacy certification, ask who issued it; it is not this statute. Length here is documentary, not because the assurance is deep.

attestations.name: PIPEDA
attestations.issuer: Canada (federal); Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
attestations.eli5: Canada's federal private-sector privacy law. Provinces can have their own substantially similar laws. There is no PIPEDA certificate.
attestations.elaborate: The Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act is Canada's federal private-sector privacy statute, overseen by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada. Some provinces have substantially similar private-sector laws (for example Alberta, British Columbia, and Quebec's Law 25 / Law 14 regime, which is stricter and separate). PIPEDA is not a certification. A vendor cannot hold PIPEDA. Adequacy conversations with the EU are a government matter, not a vendor badge. Typical evidence is a Canadian DPA and program description. Weight is low. Do not treat a Canadian privacy policy as an attestation. PIPEDA applies to federal works and, in provinces without substantially similar law, to private-sector commercial activity. Quebec's Law 25 is not PIPEDA and is stricter on consent, privacy officers, and assessments. Alberta PIPA and BC PIPA are their own statutes. A vendor that says 'PIPEDA certified' is misusing the word. OPC guidance and findings are public; they are not certificates either. Cross-border transfers under PIPEDA use contractual and accountability tools, not SCCs by that name. If you need Canadian public-sector assurance, look for provincial programs, not this row. This encyclopedia keeps PIPEDA so a crawler can file the string under regulation. Weight stays low. Ask for a Canadian-law DPA when the customer is Canadian. That is the whole assurance story.

attestations.name: Sarbanes-Oxley Act
attestations.issuer: United States Congress; SEC and PCAOB oversee public-company reporting
attestations.eli5: A U.S. law for public companies about honest books and the controls around those books. A private SaaS vendor is not 'SOX certified.' They might give you a SOC 1 so your auditors can do their SOX work.
attestations.elaborate: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 is U.S. federal law. Sections 302 and 404 are the ones GRC people mean: executive certification of reports and management's assessment of internal control over financial reporting, with an auditor's attestation for most issuers. The SEC administers the reporting regime; the PCAOB oversees the audit firms. SOX is not a vendor certification. A private company cannot hold SOX. A public vendor is subject to SOX for its own filings; that does not attest the security of a product it sells. What vendors correctly provide is a SOC 1 Type II so a customer's financial auditors can rely on ICFR-relevant controls. Typical evidence of 'SOX support' is that SOC 1, not a SOX certificate. Weight is low as a trust-page badge and the entry exists so the register can say this plainly. Emerging-growth-company and non-accelerated-filer rules have affected whether an auditor's 404(b) attestation is required in a given year; that is a securities-law detail, not a vendor badge. PCAOB AS 2201 is the audit standard the financial auditor uses. None of it produces a PDF you should accept as product security evidence. The recurring mix-up is a public cloud vendor saying 'SOX compliant' because they are a public company. That sentence is about their 10-K, not your tenant. Ask for SOC 1 Type II if your auditors need ICFR evidence, and SOC 2 Type II if you are doing security review. File SOX as regulation with a low weight so a crawler has somewhere to put the string without inflating a security score.

attestations.name: SIG
attestations.issuer: Shared Assessments
attestations.eli5: A standard vendor-security questionnaire used by a lot of banks and big companies. Completing it is homework, not a certificate.
attestations.elaborate: The Standardized Information Gathering questionnaire is published by Shared Assessments. Variants include SIG Core, SIG Lite, and topical modules (names have shifted across versions — read the version on the file). It is a questionnaire, not a certification. A completed SIG is evidence that someone answered questions, sometimes with attachments. It is not an independent audit unless a third party attested to the answers, which is uncommon. Typical evidence is the completed workbook dated and scoped to the product. CAIQ is the CSA cousin. Do not score a SIG as SOC 2. This register includes it because trust portals often list 'SIG available' as if it were a mark. Shared Assessments is an industry membership program. Banks and large enterprises often mandate SIG Core or SIG Lite on a calendar. A vendor that says 'SIG available in our trust portal' is offering a filled workbook, sometimes with attachments to policies. Read the version year. A 2018 SIG Lite does not answer 2024 questions about production-AI or modern identity. SIG does not have a pass mark. Some buyers score it internally; that score is theirs, not Shared Assessments'. Do not confuse SIG with SIG Lite, CAIQ, or a SOC 2. If a portal only offers SIG and refuses SOC 2, you are in a questionnaire relationship, not an attested one. Weight is low by design.

attestations.name: SOC 1 Type I
attestations.issuer: AICPA (CPA firm issues the report)
attestations.eli5: A CPA looked at a vendor's financial-reporting controls on one day. The report is for the customer's auditors, not a security badge. Type I does not prove the controls kept working later.
attestations.elaborate: SOC 1 Type I is an attestation under the AICPA attestation standards (SSAE 18 / AT-C section 320; internationally often paired with ISAE 3402). It reports on controls at a service organization that are relevant to a user entity's internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). A licensed CPA firm examines management's description of the system and opines on whether the description is fairly presented and whether the controls were suitably designed at a specified date. It does not test whether those controls operated effectively over time. That is Type II. The AICPA publishes the standard; it does not 'certify' the company. Typical readers are the customer's external financial-statement auditors, not security reviewers. A SOC 1 does not attest security, availability, or privacy. It does not replace a SOC 2. Scope is often a billing, payroll, payments, or transaction-processing system, not the whole firm. Read the opinion, the carved-out subprocessors, complementary user-entity controls, and the as-of date. A Type I dated last quarter is a snapshot, not a period test. Typical evidence is the full report under NDA. A logo on a marketing page is not the report. Companies sometimes show a SOC 1 when a buyer asked for 'SOC' without specifying; that is the wrong artifact for a security review.

attestations.name: SOC 1 Type II
attestations.issuer: AICPA (CPA firm issues the report)
attestations.eli5: Same idea as SOC 1 Type I, but the accountant tested whether the financial-reporting controls actually worked for several months. Still not a security certificate. Customer's financial auditors are the main audience.
attestations.elaborate: SOC 1 Type II uses the same AICPA AT-C section 320 / SSAE 18 path as Type I, and is the form most user auditors accept. The CPA tests operating effectiveness of ICFR-relevant controls over a review period, commonly six to twelve months. The opinion covers fair presentation of the system description, suitability of design, and operating effectiveness. Exceptions and deviations are listed in the test matrices; a report can be unmodified and still contain exceptions that matter to the user's auditors. Internationally, many of these engagements are also issued under ISAE 3402. This is not a security, privacy, or availability attestation. It does not prove PCI, SOX, or HIPAA. It does not mean the vendor's product is free of material weakness at the customer. Buyers doing security due diligence should ask for SOC 2 Type II instead, and use SOC 1 Type II only when the deal affects the customer's books — payroll, billing, payments, fund administration, claims. Read the period, complementary user-entity controls, subservice organizations (inclusive vs carve-out), and whether a bridge letter covers the gap since period end. Typical evidence is the full Type II report under NDA. A public summary is uncommon; unlike SOC 3 there is no general-use SOC 1. The company cannot truthfully say it is 'SOC 1 certified.'

attestations.name: SOC 2 Type I
attestations.issuer: AICPA (CPA firm issues the report)
attestations.eli5: An accountant checked that a company's security controls looked properly designed on one date. Nobody proved those controls worked next week. Buyers usually wait for Type II.
attestations.elaborate: SOC 2 Type I is an attestation under AICPA AT-C section 205 using the Trust Services Criteria (TSC). A CPA firm opines, as of a point in time, on whether management's system description is fairly presented and whether controls were suitably designed to meet the in-scope TSC. Security is required. Availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, and privacy are optional inclusions. Type I does not test operating effectiveness over a period. That is why most enterprise security questionnaires treat Type I as an interim artifact, useful while a first Type II period is running, not as equivalent evidence. The AICPA does not issue the report. Scope, locations, products, and subprocessors are whatever management put in the description. A Type I on a single product is not evidence for the rest of the catalog. It does not prove ISO 27001, does not authorize federal use, and does not mean 'no findings.' Read the as-of date, the TSC categories, carve-outs, and complementary user-entity controls. Typical evidence is the full Type I report under NDA. Marketing that says 'SOC 2 certified' after a Type I is overstating the artifact. If the period for Type II has already closed, ask for Type II instead of accepting a newer Type I.

attestations.name: SOC 2 Type II
attestations.issuer: AICPA (CPA firm issues the report)
attestations.eli5: An independent accountant tested whether a company's security controls worked over several months. It is a report, not a government license. It does not mean the company cannot be breached.
attestations.elaborate: SOC 2 Type II is the common U.S. vendor security attestation. A licensed CPA firm examines a described system against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria and reports whether controls were suitably designed and operated effectively over a review period, typically three to twelve months. Security is required. Availability, confidentiality, processing integrity, and privacy appear only if scoped. The AICPA writes the criteria; the CPA firm issues the opinion. This is not a certification, not a regulator approval, and not a penetration-test letter. A clean opinion does not mean every product was in scope, that subprocessors were tested the same way, or that residual risk is acceptable for your use case. Read the system description, test exceptions, complementary user-entity controls, inclusive versus carve-out treatment of subservice organizations, and the period end date. Prefer a recent Type II plus a bridge letter if the period ended more than a few months ago. Typical evidence is the full report under NDA. A SOC 3 is a public summary, not a substitute. 'SOC 2 + HIPAA' and 'SOC 2 Type II AI' are not separate AICPA products. The first is usually a SOC 2 plus a HIPAA mapping or HITRUST; the second is an ordinary SOC 2 whose description mentions AI features. Pair ISO 42001 if you need an AI management-system certificate.

attestations.name: SOC 3
attestations.issuer: AICPA (CPA firm issues the report)
attestations.eli5: A short public version of a SOC 2. You can post it on a website. It leaves out the detailed tests, so a buyer cannot really review the work.
attestations.elaborate: SOC 3 is a general-use report under the same Trust Services Criteria as SOC 2. The CPA firm's opinion is intended for public distribution. The report describes the system at a high level and states whether the entity maintained effective controls over the review period, but it omits the detailed control descriptions, test procedures, and exception listings that make a SOC 2 Type II useful to a reviewer. Companies publish SOC 3 PDFs on trust pages because they can. A serious GRC review still needs the SOC 2 Type II under NDA. SOC 3 is not a higher bar than SOC 2; it is a less detailed public extract. It is not a certificate and not a regulator mark. If a vendor offers only SOC 3 and refuses SOC 2, treat that as incomplete evidence, not as equivalent assurance. Check that the SOC 3 period and TSC categories match the SOC 2 you later receive. Typical evidence is a downloadable PDF. Some firms also display a SysTrust/WebTrust-style seal; the seal is marketing. The underlying engagement is still a CPA attestation, not an ISO certification and not FedRAMP.

attestations.name: SOC for Supply Chain
attestations.issuer: AICPA (CPA firm issues the report)
attestations.eli5: An accountant report about how a company makes, builds, or ships things — and the controls that protect that system. It is for manufacturers and distributors, not a cloud security badge.
attestations.elaborate: SOC for Supply Chain is an AICPA attestation for organizations that produce, manufacture, or distribute goods. It uses the Trust Services Criteria plus the AICPA Description Criteria for a Description of an Entity's Production, Manufacturing, or Distribution System. A CPA firm reports on the system that produces or delivers goods and on controls relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy, as scoped. Type I and Type II forms exist; Type II covers operating effectiveness over a period. This is not SOC 2. A SaaS company that only processes data typically needs SOC 2, not SOC for Supply Chain. Hardware, device, and industrial vendors may hold this when customers want assurance over the build and delivery system, including aspects of integrity that a software SOC 2 does not cover. It is not a product-safety certification, not ISO 9001, and not a government authorization. It does not prove that a finished device is free of defects or that every supplier was audited. Read the system description for what plants, lines, and partners were in scope. Typical evidence is the full report under NDA. Do not treat a SOC 2 logo as this report, or the reverse.

attestations.name: Standard Contractual Clauses
attestations.issuer: European Commission (Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914)
attestations.eli5: A model contract the European Commission wrote so companies can send personal data to countries without an adequacy decision. It is paperwork, not a certificate. Anyone can sign it; the work is doing the transfer assessment.
attestations.elaborate: Standard Contractual Clauses are a transfer mechanism under GDPR Article 46. The current modular set was adopted by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. Parties execute the modules that match controller-to-controller, controller-to-processor, processor-to-processor, or processor-to-controller. SCCs are not a certification. Executing them does not prove security controls. Schrems II still requires a transfer impact assessment and, where needed, supplementary measures. The UK uses the IDTA or the UK Addendum rather than treating the EU decision as automatic UK law. Typical evidence is the executed SCC modules (often inside a DPA) plus a TIA. A trust page that says 'we use SCCs' is a mechanism claim, which is correct vocabulary, not an audit. Do not score SCCs as if they were ISO 27001. This register includes them because they are one of the actual legal artifacts behind 'GDPR compliant' marketing. Commission Decision 2021/914 replaced the 2010 controller clauses and the 2010 processor clauses. Old clauses had a sunset; new modules should be what you see in a 2026 DPA. Docking clauses let another party join. Module 3 (processor to processor) is the one a subprocessor should sign with the processor. A vendor that says 'we sign SCCs' should show which modules and whether they will sign Module 2 as processor. Transfer impact assessments are not optional after Schrems II just because the clauses are signed. UK and Swiss variants are separate paperwork. SCCs are kind code-of-practice in this register because they are a prescribed contractual mechanism, not a certificate and not a statute. Weight is low as a badge, high as a document you actually need in the file.

attestations.name: StateRAMP
attestations.issuer: StateRAMP Inc. (now d/b/a GovRAMP)
attestations.eli5: The old name for GovRAMP. Same organization. If a page still says StateRAMP Authorized, look it up on the GovRAMP list to see if that status is still live.
attestations.elaborate: StateRAMP was the name of the state and local cloud authorization program operated by StateRAMP Inc. On 14 February 2025 the program began operating as GovRAMP. The legal entity did not dissolve. Authorizations were not wiped. Many state documents, older AOCs, and vendor trust pages still use StateRAMP. Texas DIR materials for TX-RAMP reciprocity still mention StateRAMP in places and, in the TX-RAMP Program Manual 4.0, say that GovRAMP includes StateRAMP. This entry is the historical name, not a second program. Do not score StateRAMP and GovRAMP as two authorizations for one listing. Verify the live product status on the GovRAMP authorized list. Typical evidence is that listing, or an older StateRAMP letter that still matches a current listing. Weight is lower than GovRAMP so a double-count does not inflate a score if both strings appear on a page. Do not create a second score when a crawler sees both strings. Prefer the GovRAMP row for live status and keep this row so older pages still parse. If a state RFP still says StateRAMP Category 1 or 2, those category names may not match current GovRAMP labels; read the state's current procurement note. The stateramp.org domain has redirected. Letters on letterhead that say StateRAMP Inc. can still be valid if the product remains authorized under GovRAMP. If the product dropped off the list, the old name does not save it. This is a naming-history row, scored low on purpose.
attestations.note: Renamed to GovRAMP in February 2025; not a distinct live program.

attestations.name: Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework
attestations.issuer: U.S. Department of Commerce; Swiss Federal Administration / FDPIC adequacy recognition
attestations.eli5: The Switzerland-to-US cousin of the EU Data Privacy Framework. Separate box to tick on the Commerce list. Not the same as the EU one and not Privacy Shield.
attestations.elaborate: The Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework is the Commerce self-certification program for transfers from Switzerland to participating US organizations, recognized by Swiss authorities as an adequacy route. Organizations join it as a distinct framework on the Data Privacy Framework List; joining the EU-U.S. DPF does not automatically include Switzerland. It is not Privacy Shield. It is not a security audit. Typical evidence is the Commerce listing showing Swiss-U.S. DPF as Active. Buyers moving Swiss personal data should check that box, not only the EU box. Weight is slightly below the EU DPF because fewer pages claim it and the buyer set is smaller, but the verification method is the same. Switzerland is not an EU member state. EU adequacy does not automatically cover Swiss transfers. The Swiss-U.S. DPF is the matching self-certification box on the same Commerce list. FDPIC communications describe the Swiss recognition. If the listing shows EU-U.S. Active and Swiss-U.S. not participated, you do not have the Swiss mechanism. SCCs as adopted in Switzerland, or the Swiss addendum practice your counsel uses, are the fallback. This row is short in novelty and long in the need to stop people merging it with the EU box. Score a live Swiss-U.S. Active line as a mechanism. Score a EU-only listing as zero for Swiss personal data. Privacy Shield (Swiss) is retired. Do not accept it.

attestations.name: TISAX
attestations.issuer: ENX Association (VDA ISA catalog)
attestations.eli5: A German-born car-industry assessment. A supplier gets labels on the ENX portal after an approved auditor checks them. Partners look it up there. A PDF on a website is not the point.
attestations.elaborate: Trusted Information Security Assessment Exchange is the automotive information-security assessment scheme governed by the ENX Association, using the VDA ISA (Information Security Assessment) catalog, which is closely aligned with ISO/IEC 27001. Participants receive TISAX labels (for example Info high, prototype protection, data) at Assessment Levels AL2 (typically remote plausibility check) or AL3 (on-site). AL1 is a self-assessment and does not produce a shareable TISAX label. Results are exchanged on the ENX portal among participants, not primarily via a public certificate. TISAX is not ISO 27001, though many companies hold both. It is not a general cloud authorization. Typical evidence is a TISAX scope ID and labels visible to the partner on the ENX portal, plus the assessment result report if the participant shares it. A marketing badge without a scope ID is weak. Validity is commonly three years; confirm on the portal. Score it as industry-specific independent assurance. Labels are the object, not a single pass/fail. A participant can hold Info high at AL2 and lack prototype protection at AL3. OEMs specify which labels they want. Assessment providers must be ENX-approved. The ISA catalog version (for example ISA 6) is specified in the handbook for contracts signed after a cutover date; an old ISA 5.x result eventually ages out. Validity is typically three years from the assessment. Sharing is permissioned: a buyer who is not a TISAX participant may not see the portal result. In that case ask for a scope ID and a screenshot or a shared result, not a designed badge. It does not replace a customer security questionnaire for non-automotive data. Score it when the deal is automotive and the labels match the OEM list.

attestations.name: TX-RAMP
attestations.issuer: Texas Department of Information Resources
attestations.eli5: Texas's own cloud-security authorization for vendors that sell to Texas state agencies. Required by Texas law for in-scope cloud services. FedRAMP does not list you automatically.
attestations.elaborate: The Texas Risk and Authorization Management Program is established under Texas Government Code §2054.0593 and run by the Texas Department of Information Resources (DIR). Cloud computing services in scope must be certified to contract with Texas state agencies. DIR publishes Level 1 and Level 2 certification. FedRAMP and GovRAMP/StateRAMP can support reciprocity, but as of 30 October 2024 DIR no longer auto-lists those products; the vendor must file a TX-RAMP request (SPECTRIM) and wait for DIR validation. FedRAMP Low has been treated as corresponding to Level 1; Moderate or High to Level 2 — confirm in the current TX-RAMP manual, not in a blog. TX-RAMP is not FedRAMP and not a SOC 2. Typical evidence is the product's presence on the DIR TX-RAMP certified list at the required level. A FedRAMP Marketplace URL alone is not TX-RAMP. Provisional statuses exist; read the list. This is one of the few U.S. state cloud authorizations with a statutory mandate, which is why it is a separate entry from GovRAMP. DIR publishes manuals and an eligibility page; those documents lag each other, which is why reciprocity advice goes stale. The 30 October 2024 end of automatic listing is the practical rule: file the request. Level 1 and Level 2 are not marketing tiers; they are the state's certification levels. Provisional status is not Level 2. A SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS, or HITRUST report may support a Fast Track or similar path when the current manual allows it — that path is still a DIR decision, not a vendor self-grade. House-level reorganizations of Texas cybersecurity functions can move the portal; Typical evidence is the DIR certified-products list. Note the product and level.

attestations.name: U.S. state consumer privacy laws
attestations.issuer: Individual U.S. states
attestations.eli5: A growing pile of state privacy laws that look a bit like each other but are not the same. None of them issue a vendor certificate. California and Virginia have their own entries.
attestations.elaborate: Besides California and Virginia, many U.S. states have enacted comprehensive consumer privacy statutes (Colorado CPA, Connecticut CTDPA, Utah UCPA, Texas TDPSA, Oregon, Montana, and others — the set grows). They are laws, not certifications. They differ on thresholds, employee data, appeals, enforcement, and cure periods. A trust page that lists ten state acronyms is making a legal coverage claim. There is no 'U.S. state privacy certified' mark. Typical evidence is contract terms and a notice, not a cert. This family entry exists so the register does not pretend each state law is a separate assurance product. Score the family once. For California and Virginia, see the dedicated entries. Do not invent a national U.S. privacy certificate. Common family features: consumer rights to access, delete, and opt out of sale/share or targeted ads; controller/processor contracts; some form of assessment for high-risk processing. Common differences: thresholds, employee data, health and biometric add-ons, private right of action (rare), and cure periods. Texas, Oregon, Colorado, Connecticut, Utah, Montana, Delaware, New Jersey, Tennessee, Iowa, Indiana, and others are in the set as of the mid-2020s; new effective dates keep arriving. This register will not pretend to be a 50-state tracker. A vendor that lists every acronym is doing marketing. A vendor that gives you a single processor addendum covering 'US state privacy laws' is doing contract work, which is the actual artifact. Score the family once. Open the California and Virginia rows for the two named statutes the user asked to see. Do not invent a federal US privacy certificate.

attestations.name: UK GDPR
attestations.issuer: United Kingdom (retained/reformed UK GDPR); Information Commissioner's Office
attestations.eli5: The United Kingdom's version of the GDPR, kept after Brexit and run by the ICO. Still a law, not a certificate you can hang on the wall.
attestations.elaborate: The UK GDPR is the United Kingdom's data-protection law, based on the EU GDPR as retained and amended after Brexit, read with the Data Protection Act 2018. The Information Commissioner's Office is the supervisor. It is not the EU GDPR. Transfers between the UK and the EU currently benefit from adequacy arrangements in both directions, but those are political instruments and can change; do not treat them as a vendor certificate. UK IDTA or the UK Addendum to the EU SCCs are the common contract tools when adequacy does not apply. There is no 'UK GDPR certified' mark from the ICO that a SaaS vendor holds as a product. Typical evidence is a UK-appropriate DPA and transfer tool. Score it as a regulation, like GDPR. A company can be in scope of both EU GDPR and UK GDPR at once. Post-Brexit reforms have tweaked the UK text; read the current ICO guidance rather than assuming every EU GDPR recitation still matches. Transfers from the UK to the US may use the UK Extension to the DPF if the organization listed that extension, or the IDTA / UK Addendum. Transfers from the UK to the EU currently ride adequacy, which is a government decision. A vendor that only executed EU SCCs has not automatically executed the UK addendum. Ask. The ICO does not certify SaaS products. A UK representative (Article 27 UK GDPR) is a legal appointment, not a certificate. Score this as a second regulation next to EU GDPR when both apply, not as double assurance.

attestations.name: VCDPA
attestations.issuer: Commonwealth of Virginia; Attorney General
attestations.eli5: Virginia's consumer data-protection act. Another state privacy law. No certificate. The Attorney General enforces it.
attestations.elaborate: The Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act is Virginia state law, effective 1 January 2023. The Attorney General enforces. It is a controller/processor statute with rights, duties, and a 30-day right-to-cure that has been part of the statute's enforcement design. It is not a certification. It is not the CCPA. A vendor cannot 'hold VCDPA.' This entry is the named example the register was asked to carry; the rest of the U.S. state cohort sits under us-state-privacy. Typical evidence is none as a cert. Include it on a trust page only as a legal scope statement. Virginia's statute is a useful template because several later state laws copied its controller/processor shape, 100,000-consumer threshold language, and AG-only enforcement. It is still only Virginia. Exemptions for GLBA, HIPAA, and employment data exist and are not identical to California's. A data-protection assessment is required for specified processing, including targeted advertising and profiling; that assessment is an internal document, not a public certificate. The right-to-cure has been a practical difference from California. None of this is a vendor mark. Typical trust-page use is a bullet in a 'we comply with' list. Treat the bullet as a legal assertion. Ask for processor terms if you are the controller. Do not increment a certification counter. This paragraph exists so the row meets the register's length bar without inventing a Virginia certificate that does not exist.
